journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.* Thursday night I sent Gina the name: Mary Catherine. At breakfast Nonna said *Maria Caterina* nine times, and cried the good kind, and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. Candlemas: she took a Giant Eagle bag of tapers to St. Brigid’s to be blessed at the door, one for every room and every one of us, like every February second since she was a bride. And one more, *per Maria Caterina*. Father Dom asked who. She told him. He blessed it.

body: The window over the Lagoon has gone from black to a gray with nothing in it yet, and on the desk the RAZR is walking itself toward the edge on its own vibration, one ring at a time. Jack gets a hand over it before the drop. The little outside window says GLENWOOD.
Theo is a long shape under the comforter on the far side of the room. On the nightstand Hollis keeps the watch from his teacup.
Jack takes it to the window in his socks and flips it open. “It’s quarter to ten here and I’ve been to Mass,” Ma says. “What have you done?”
“I’m getting there.”

“I’m in the vestibule. It’s the one place in the building with no children in it.” Behind her a door lets the cold in, and a pair of boots goes by on the tile at the walk of somebody who has been told to walk. “It’s Candlemas. Nonna brought the bag.”
“The Giant Eagle bag.”

“The big paper one, with the handles. She stood at the holy water holding it open like a child on Halloween, and Father Dom blessed it all at once, tapers and bag. One for every room in the house and one for every person in it, same as every second of February since she was a bride.” She steps away from the door. “She keeps them in the drawer with the matches. For weather. Don’t ask me.”

body.text: “And one more,” Ma says. “*Per Maria Caterina.* Father Dom asked her who. She told him. He blessed it.”
body.else: “And one more,” Ma says, “for the girl on the television. Father Dom blessed it. Don’t ask me.”

body: She doesn’t say anything else about it. On the line there is the vestibule: a radiator, the boots again, a child being told not to blow on it.
Jack sits down on the footlocker. “What did Father Dom say?”

“He said *amen*, Jackie. It’s a candle.” Somewhere behind her, through two sets of doors, Nonna is explaining the correct way to hold a taper to someone in dialect, at a volume that carries. “She says blessed wax burns slower. Your father timed one in the garage once, with a stopwatch from the plant. He won’t say how it came out, and he lights them every year.”
“What about Rosie?”

“Rosie carried hers in the school procession with both hands and her tongue out, and the principal said it was the most reverent walk in the history of the building. Rosie was watching the fire.” The boots go by. “Your brother is twenty-three today.”
“I know, Ma.”
“I know you know. I’m saying it in a church, so it counts.”
Down on the Lagoon a man in waders is walking a dog that doesn’t want to go, and Jack gives the pair of them his full attention.
“The card’s in Gina’s envelope. It went Monday.”
“It’ll be there Friday. Saturday, with the sorting. Write him again, Jackie. Two letters beats one card.”
“Your father looks up the weather out there every morning on the Dell, before Gina’s up. He says sixty degrees in February is an insult.”
“It’s fifty-eight.”
“He’ll take that as a second one.”

The RAZR buzzes twice against his ear. “That’s your sister,” Ma says. “It’s in her sock. Second period they collect them in a basket, and she hands in the old one. Don’t answer, they can hear it through the sock.”
He takes the phone from his ear and holds it out in front of him, still on the line.

body: He says it in his head, to be safe: *Happy birthday, Danny.* It takes more standing still than he expected.

“Your father wants a word,” Ma says. “Frank. He won’t come in, he says the heater’s on.” She shoulders the outer door open and the cold comes down the line, and under it an engine idling rough, forty feet from her, that Jack would know in a parking structure. The Silverado. She holds the phone out toward it at the length of her arm.
“Morning, Pop,” Jack says.
A pause, the length of a man deciding about a window. Then, small and close, from inside a cab: “Rodent saw his shadow.”
“Frank,” Ma says.
“Six more weeks.” The engine coughs under it. “Like we needed a rodent.”
“It’s two hours from the house, Jackie,” Ma says over it. “He takes it personally.”
“Tell him the truck started.”
“He can hear you, Frank. It’s a telephone.”

The door comes back across the tile, and the line is only the vestibule again. From the far bed, from under the comforter, without any part of him moving, Theo says, “Is that your mother? Tell her Hollis sends his love.”
“Theo says Hollis sends his love.”
“Hollis is in the Mass intentions,” Ma says. “Whatever he is.”

body.text: From the comforter Theo adds: “Hollis would like it noted that you never answered him Sunday. Hollis worried.”
body.else: From the comforter Theo adds: “Hollis says thank you for coming home Sunday.”

body: The comforter comes down to one eye. It is open all the way; at five to seven it has done that maybe twice since September. “Breakfast,” Theo says. “I’m buying. The Anchor. Seven-forty; I’ve timed the walk.” The eye holds on Jack. “Wear the face you use for priests.”
Jack doesn’t answer him. He has a mother on the line and a theory about men who offer to buy breakfast and specify the face. The comforter goes back up.
“Jackie.” Ma is back at the doorway. “I’m writing him tonight, the long one. Whatever you want in it, say it now and I’ll put it in.”

choices.text: “Tell him happy birthday from the beach.”
response: “He’ll like that,” Ma says. “He’ll pretend he doesn’t.”
A cough in the vestibule, and a child told to walk. Through the inner doors, from the front pew, comes the small steady click of Nonna’s beads against the wood: a click, and a click.

choices.text: “Tell Pop the rodent’s from Pennsylvania. It doesn’t count.”
response: Ma carries it out the door. “Frank. Jackie says the rodent’s from Pennsylvania. It doesn’t count.”
A window going down. The idle, clearer. “That’s what I said.”
“That’s what he said,” Ma tells Jack, in case he missed it. Across the lot the Silverado’s horn goes off once, short, and the line fills with the sound of her walking back in.

choices.text: “Light Danny’s for me. Tonight.”
response: “I was going to light his tonight,” Ma says. “Now it’s from you.” A breath comes down the line from Ohio. “Did you eat?”
“Theo’s buying.”
“That isn’t a yes.”
“It’s a plan.”
“Then eat something,” she says, and the vestibule gives it back to her off the tile before the line closes.

s02.slug: TUESDAY · 7:40 AM · THE ANCHOR — THE BACK BOOTH
body: The Anchor has the harbor in every window and the Saints on the radio. Over the register a man from Metairie is telling a host who has stopped interrupting him that he has waited forty-three years, and the host says, “Take your time, sir,” and the man takes all of it.

Theo is in the back booth with his back to the wall and his blazer on the hook, and across from him a second cup is already turned up on its saucer. He has ordered for both of them: in Theo’s case, two of everything that comes with toast.
“There it is,” he says, as Jack slides in. “The face. I knew you had it on you.”
Gloria has the mornings until the day girl’s baby makes up its mind, and she has given the baby till Friday. She has the pot over Jack’s cup before he is all the way into the booth.
“Your professor sat in that booth till two in the morning Sunday,” she says, pouring. “Reading me Housman. I put him in a cab.”

Jack looks at the bench, and the ketchup, and the harbor in the window behind Theo’s head. Then he sits down in it. At the pass Rudy has his transistor on a man selling tires in Spanish, in open competition with the Saints.

body.text: Going away with the pot she says, “And tell your peach she still owes me a verdict on the lattice.”

body: Theo waits for the pot to be out of earshot. Then he moves the creamer, the Tabasco and his own plate to the windowsill, one at a time, and clears the table down to the two paper placemats the Anchor puts out: the harbor chart on the left, soundings and shoals and a lighthouse with a halo of little rays, and on the right the month’s tide table in columns.

Across the chart, in green-black ink, in the small even hand he keeps for contracts and condolence notes, runs an outline with arrows. COLD OPEN. ACT ONE. ACT TWO. ACT THREE. Beside the last one somebody has drawn a very good crown. The fountain pen is uncapped in his hand.
“I’ve prepared a document,” Theo says.
“It’s a placemat.”

“It’s a treatment, on a placemat, which is how every great picture starts. I would have used a napkin, but the Anchor’s napkins give way under ink. Questions after the third act, my moral compass.” The pen touches the first line. “Cold open. A city that has never won anything.”
“They haven’t won yet,” Jack says.

“The treatment isn’t concerned with that. A treatment doesn’t pitch the movie where they lose.” The pen moves down. “Act one: Super Bowl Sunday at the Broussards’. A television, a grandmother with views on the offensive line, a number of cousins I have chosen not to count. Act two: the week the city can’t go back to work. Offices closed in sympathy with themselves. Act three —” he lowers his voice, as to a congregation — “Bacchus. Drew Brees, Costigan. Quarterback of a championship and king of a parade, seven days apart. That is the Holy Roman Empire.”
“Voltaire said the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.”
“Voltaire never saw a king throw a spiral. Working title: *Who Dat*.”
“That’s a chant.”
“It’s a franchise, Costigan. Everything is, eventually. Casting is complete. You, Father Jack, are the skeptical young cleric who wanders in confused and ends up on a float.”
“I’m not going on a float.”
“The treatment is flexible about floats.”

From the inside pocket of the blazer he takes a fan of paper, striped faintly at the edges by a Delgado-lab printer running low on toner, and deals it onto the tide table one sheet at a time. Jack reads the names upside down. VANCE. PRICE. BROUSSARD. TRAN. LINDQVIST. COSTIGAN. The last one Theo turns around to face him.

body: “Six seats,” Theo says. “Out of Santa Barbara Friday at 1:15, through Dallas, into New Orleans by ten, in time for leftovers, and leftovers in that house are a meal. Home Monday the fifteenth. Paid. Printed. I am now on a first-name basis with the lab monitor, who believes I work for the State Department.” He taps the sheet. “Celeste Broussard has made up the twins’ room.”
“Tran?” Jack says.
“Kevin’s grandmother has decreed Tết at a church in New Orleans East, on pain of ceasing to be his grandmother, or he her grandson; the decree was unclear.”
“Lindqvist?”
“Margot is coming for science.”
“What science?”
“Parades. She has a position. It’s footnoted.” The pen goes down to the margin. “The musician isn’t going. It’s her city. It isn’t his.”
“I don’t care what Julian’s doing.”
“That’s why I said it fast.”
“Ten days,” Jack says. “In her mother’s house.”
“A very large house with a very serious kitchen.”
“It’s the week before Lent.”
“Which is why it exists. The Church throws the party so the fast has something to be about. You of all people should respect a feast that’s honest about what comes next.”
“I respect it from here. I don’t own a shirt for a city that’s seventy in February.”
“You own a Carhartt, which is a linen jacket in a lower tax bracket. We’ll adapt.”
“I have class. I have Gloria’s Saturdays.”
“Gloria has survived worse than your absence. She has survived the lunch rush.”
“And you paid.”
“I did.”
“That’s worse.”
“It’s called a gift, Costigan.”
“A gift is something you can say no to.”
“You can.” The pen is still. “I’d rather you didn’t.”
“And I’m not leaving Skye for ten days.”
“She would tell you to go,” Theo says. “She’d have a speech. It would be very good.”
“That’s not why.”
“I know why.”
He lays the pen across the harbor chart with the nib off the paper, so it won’t blot, and there is nothing in his hands. On the radio the man from Metairie is thanked for his call.
“Costigan. I’m asking.”
Jack waits for the rest: the turn, the closing logline.
“For me,” Theo says.
“Theo —”
“I’ve never asked you for anything.”
Jack goes back through five months of Theo, every coat and ticket and favor going the other way, looking for the one time, and it isn’t there.
“I need you there.”

“No.”
Theo doesn’t argue it. He turns the COSTIGAN ticket face down on the tide table with one finger, and the other five lie there looking up at the ceiling fan.

response: Theo looks at him across the two placemats until the next caller, from Kenner, has gotten through his first sentence.
“Anything,” he says, as though writing it on his cuff. He caps the fountain pen.

choices.key: Over the Anchor’s placemats, the first thing Theo has ever asked you for: New Orleans. You asked for a postcard of the king. Then you said no.
response: Theo laughs, one bark of it, delighted and appalled. Jack waits for it to be over and then says it, under the end of it: “No, Theo.”
The laugh doesn’t finish. Theo squares the stack of tickets so the edges meet.

response: Nothing comes after it. Theo nods, as if he has been given a note on a scene he loves, and looks at the harbor window instead of at Jack.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed. Tuesday morning she had the day girl’s shift. Hale sat in our booth till two Sunday morning reading her Housman; she put him in a cab. Theo pitched me New Orleans on her placemats. She rated it a meringue: all air, and it still costs four dollars.

body: Theo folds the harbor chart in thirds, arrows and crown and all, and slips it into the blazer on the hook. The six tickets go in after it.
“It’s refundable,” he says.
Jack, who read the bottom line of the page that is now in Theo’s pocket, says nothing.
“Fully,” Theo says. “American has a heart, Costigan; it’s in their charter. Mid-cabin, by the wing. I can have it back by lunch.”
They both look at the sugar.
Gloria is wiping down the next booth with a rag. She doesn’t look at Theo; she looks at the corner of the placemat still showing at the edge of the blazer, a tail of blue-gray harbor.
“That was a meringue, hon. All air, and it still costs four dollars.”
“I’m told that’s a compliment in some cities,” Theo says.
“Not in this one.”
At the end of the counter Merle says “Meringue” to his eggs and goes back to eating them.
He pays for both with a fifty on a thirteen-dollar check and is out the door before the saucer stops turning.

Outside, the wharf is doing its morning: a forklift backing a pallet of crates toward the fish house, beeping its way along, the ice machine at the fish house dumping a load with a sound like a car wreck, a gull on every piling. Theo walks half a block with his hands in the blazer pockets and the folded chart a flat shape against his ribs, and says nothing, and it is a quiet Jack could measure in squid crates. Twice Jack starts a sentence with Theo’s name in it and drops it on the sidewalk. At the corner, without turning his head, Theo is Theo about something else entirely.
“Pruitt has drawn the island to scale,” he says. “There is no scale. The island doesn’t have a scale, Costigan, that’s the premise. He used a ruler.”

s03.slug: TUESDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — CANDLEMAS
body: By noon the sun comes straight down through the olive trees, and that is hard on candles. In full California light a taper is hardly there: the flame goes clear, and what you see is the air above it shaking and the wax going soft in somebody’s fist.

Father Osei is at a card table by the fountain in white vestments, sprinkling a drift of tapers with holy water and the unhurried confidence of a man watering a lawn. At the end of the table a boy of about six in a clip-on tie has discovered that the bulletin burns. He holds it up to show the courtyard. His mother takes the bulletin, the taper and then, after a short and visible negotiation, the boy. On the backswing the sprinkler gets Jack across the cheekbone. “Ɛyɛ,” Osei says mildly, not looking up from the tapers. “It is well. It begins on the outside.”

Kevin has the candle box. It’s a flat carton from a church-supply house in Ohio, and Jack decides to take it as a greeting. Kevin is handing out its contents one at a time, with eye contact, in the order people are standing.
“Jack.”
“Kev.”
“Plain or drip-guard? The drip-guards have the little paper skirt. I recommend them for anyone who’s had a week.”
“Plain.”
“Plain.” Kevin counts out two and closes Jack’s hand around both. “Take two. Everybody has somebody. I also have a candle pun.”
“Don’t.”

“Father vetoed it. Twice.” He is already smiling at the next person in line, sunny and exact, and he doesn’t say a word about Hale’s. It has the look of something decided in advance and kept as carefully as the carton.

Beside him Clare Dominguez, a violin case strapped to her back like a second, flatter coat, lights the tapers off the one Kevin holds up, a tall one, steady at the height of everybody’s hands. Each wick takes at its own speed. Clare puts hers to his and waits out the damp ones and the cheap ones and a sophomore’s shaking one, and Kevin’s hand does not move at all.
Becca Lindell turns from the line with her own flame held out in front of her and lights Jack’s off it before he can get to Clare. A drop of wax lands on his knuckle and hardens.
“Happy Candlemas, Jack.”
“Happy Candlemas, Becca.”

Across the courtyard, under the far olive, Lena has two lit tapers in one hand. A little girl in a puffy coat is crying over a candle that’s gone out, and Lena bends and gives her one of hers, flame first, and straightens, and goes in with the other. Jack doesn’t look for her. He sees it the way he sees the wax on his knuckle.

Gus Ferreira keeps his hands off the organ. Eight voices start the chant at the church door with nothing under them, a tune that climbs one step and sets itself down, and the procession goes in beneath it with the tapers carried low, as the children were told. In the doorway the draft off the center aisle takes Jack’s flame in one breath. Becca, two people behind him, leans around and lights it again off hers without comment.

St. Brendan’s is a hull turned over, and the A-frame takes the chant up into its beams and gives it back a half-second late. The procession fills the pews with small lights and the smell of struck wax. Jack kneels at the back on the Joseph side. She’s ten pews up on the Mary side.
The Gospel is Simeon and the baby and the old woman who never left the temple. Osei closes the book, lays his hands on either side of the ambo, and uses no notes.

“Simeon waited his whole life to hold one child,” he says, “and when he had held him, he asked to be let go. Not for more. To go.” The church waits with him. “And Anna, who never left the temple at all. I believe they tried to send her home.” A ripple goes through the pews. “Waiting is not wasted on God. It is only very boring for us.”
In the third row the boy in the clip-on tie says “Yes,” with feeling, and is hushed. Osei sits down.

At Communion the pews empty up the center, a row at a time. His row stands and files out past his knees. The line comes back down the side aisle and passes the end of his pew, where he’s kneeling. He hasn’t gone up. The cardigan goes by the end of the pew at the same speed as everybody else’s coat.

When the church has thinned toward the courtyard he crosses to the Mary side. The votive rack is a steel frame of glass cups over a tray of sand, and half the cups are already lit, for the sick and the missing and the dead. Jack takes the second taper out of his jacket and tips its wick to the flame of the first. It’s a cheap wick, and it takes slowly. When it has taken he stands it in the sand, a little apart from the others, with the wax going soft under his thumbnail.
Twenty-three. He has nothing to say about it that Danny would let him get away with.

s04.slug: TUESDAY · 3:50 PM · STATE STREET AT CARRILLO — THE SAAB, TOP DOWN
body: February hasn’t reached State Street. The sun is out the length of it, a man in cargo shorts is walking a bulldog in a cable-knit sweater past a store that sells nothing but olive oil, and the palms over the sidewalk stand around in the light like they’re waiting to be tipped. Two hours from Glenwood Avenue a groundhog saw his shadow this morning. Out here the Saab’s top is down. It’s been down since section.

She was at the curb when he came out of section, sitting up on the back of the driver’s seat with her sneakers on the cushion and the engine running, vibrating along with it. She didn’t say hello. She said, “I need a coat. I’ve never owned a real coat. You’re from a cold place, you have to come tell me if it’s a coat.” When he had one leg in she said, “I booked it,” and put the car in first, and he got the rest of himself in on the way to the 101.

She told him on the freeway, with the wind taking every third word off the top of her head and throwing it at the oil platforms. He got one thing of his own in somewhere along the water — noon Mass, the candles, a taper at the Mary side for Danny, twenty-three today — and she reached over and squeezed his knee and went straight back to New Mexico. She told him again in the store, from inside a sheepskin coat with a collar you could lose a cat in, walking it up and down in front of the three-way mirror. Now the coat is in a bag on the back seat and they’re at a meter on State with the engine off, and she’s telling him a third time, because as far as he can tell it hasn’t taken on her yet.

“It’s called *Caliche*.” She has both hands on top of the wheel and her chin on her hands. “It’s a kind of dirt. Hard dirt, out in the desert, like a floor somebody poured. It’s cable, it’s an hour, it’s a sheriff in a border town and his daughter, and the daughter’s me, and her name is Dell Harlan.” She sits up. “And she isn’t nice to anybody, Jack. Not one person. She has a horse and she isn’t nice to the horse.”
“Where’s the horse?”

“Outside Santa Fe. Seven thousand feet. It *snows*.” She says it like a word from a language she’s just started taking. “A car comes Saturday at six. Burbank, Albuquerque, and then some van with the show’s name taped in the window. Back the twenty-first.” She counts it off on the wheel, fingers and then fingers again. “Sixteen days.”

He has seen her be Cassidy on Nonna’s television on a Thursday: the good girl, with the hair, who says the right thing in the last two minutes. He has never seen her want anything the way she wants this girl in the snow who isn’t nice to her horse.
“You’re going to scare the hell out of New Mexico,” he says.

“My mother wanted me to pass.” She fishes the Sharpie out of the cup holder and caps it and uncaps it. She does Debbie, one line, the vowels sweet and sharp at once: “*Baby. Cassidy pays for the house.*” And herself again. “The house is paid for. I paid for it. That isn’t what she means.” She puts the key in and doesn’t turn it. “What if I can’t do it? Mean. I’ve never been anybody’s bad news. I don’t know where you keep it.”
“You took it anyway,” Jack says.
“I took it anyway.” She turns the key, and the Saab coughs and catches, and she says it again over the engine, like she wants to hear how it sounds with noise under it.
“Your turn,” she says. “I’ve been talking since the freeway.”

So he tells her about breakfast. The Anchor’s placemats with Theo’s fountain pen all over the tide table; six tickets out of the Delgado lab printer, one with COSTIGAN on it, paid for; the game at the Broussards’, a week of New Orleans, then Bacchus and a quarterback who gets to be king. Ten days. And then Theo putting the pen down and asking him — for himself, he said. Theo doesn’t ask.
“Ted pitched you on a *placemat*.”
“With an act structure.”
“Of course with an act structure.” She doesn’t laugh. She looks out at the street, at the bulldog coming back the other way in its sweater.
“Go,” she says. “Watch your Saints win it in their own city.” A bus goes by, and she waits for it. “Who knows — maybe it’ll be good for you guys.”
She leaves it at *you guys*.
“Friday’s yours,” he says.
“I leave at six on Saturday.”
“I know.”
She takes her sunglasses off and looks at him across the gearshift for a while. Then she puts them back on and puts the Saab in gear.

Carrillo is red. Carrillo is always red; the town is built to stop you there. She reaches over and turns the radio up, and the man on the station says something about the weekend, and the song comes on: the slow wet synthesizer, the falsetto, a snare like somebody tapping on the car window with one fingernail. Every Costigan alive would change the station.
“Oh no,” Jack says.
“Oh, *yes*.” She turns it up again. “It’s your brother’s birthday.”
“That’s not what it’s about.”
“I know *exactly* what it’s about.”

She starts it alone, to him, over the gearshift, one finger keeping time on the wheel. He holds out for most of the first verse with his arms folded. The hook comes around and he’s in it with her, at the top of his lungs, both of them, *birthday sex* — on Candlemas, with the noon Mass’s wax still under his thumbnail, at a red light on State Street, eyes on each other.

In the next lane there’s a silver Camry with a girl about Skye’s age at the wheel and a Flip camera held up over her steering wheel, its little red light on, pointed at them. Jack sees it between one line and the next.
“Should she even be *driving* that?” he yells over the chorus. The radio’s been full of Toyotas all week, and somewhere on Glenwood Avenue Frank Costigan is saying nothing about it, loudly.
Skye sees the camera. She keeps singing, to Jack. The light stays red. The Flip stays up.

choices.text: *Sing every word.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street you and Skye sang “Birthday Sex” at each other, top down, every word. A girl in the next lane filmed it.
response: He knows every word. This is news to both of them. He couldn’t tell you where he learned it — the Delgado laundry room, the showers on four with Pruitt’s radio on the sink, Rudy turning the Anchor’s radio up for this one song and no other — but it’s all in there, the verses, the part where the man explains himself in detail, and he sings every bit of it at her with his hand on his heart and no shame left anywhere in him.

Skye lets go of the wheel to conduct. Both hands, up over the windshield, the sunglasses sliding down her nose. She points at him for the high part, and he goes for it and misses it by a state, and she points again, and he goes again.

The light’s been green a while. He finds this out from the horns: the Camry first, then a bakery van behind them, then what sounds like most of Carrillo. Skye lets the clutch out with no gas, and the Saab bucks once and dies in the crosswalk.
“Clutch,” he says.
“I *know* where the clutch is.”
“In. Now first. Little gas — now ease off —”
“Are you teaching *me* —”
“Ease off. Easy.”

She gets it, and they lurch across Carrillo on the yellow with the song still going and the Camry honking behind them in time, and Jack is grinning at the whole of State Street like a man let out of somewhere early.

choices.text: *Do the backup vocals. All of them.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street you and Skye sang “Birthday Sex” at each other, top down — you did every backup vocal. A girl in the next lane filmed it.
response: He does the backup vocals. All of them. Every echo under her line, every *yeah*, the little answering *oh* at the back of each bar, the ad-libs nobody has ever sung on purpose, and for the falsetto he can’t hit and never will he puts a hand over his heart and shuts his eyes and tries anyway.

At the second *yeah* she folds over the wheel and can’t come back up, and he carries the song alone for two lines in a range God did not give him, until she’s back, wiping her eyes under the sunglasses, and takes it from him at the hook.

In the Camry the girl takes one hand off the wheel and gives them a thumbs-up out her window, the Flip steady in the other. The light changes. Skye takes them across Carrillo doing the outro, both parts of it, her elbow up on the door, and Jack does the echoes half a step behind her till the next light.

choices.text: *Sing it to her, not at her.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street you and Skye sang “Birthday Sex” to each other, top down, eyes on each other the whole time. A girl in the next lane filmed it.
response: He sings it to her. The filthiest song on the radio, and he sings it across the gearshift the way Pop sings Sinatra in the garage when he thinks the house is asleep: slow, a little behind the band, every line a thing he’s handing over. It’s ridiculous. He does it anyway, and he doesn’t look at the Camry once.

Halfway through the second verse she stops clowning. She turns in her seat to face him, one knee up against the gearshift, and sings the next line back to him, and the one after it, at the top of her lungs and straight at him, and in the next lane the girl behind the Flip has gone quiet to watch.

The light goes green, and neither of them notices till the horn behind them, long. She drives across Carrillo one-handed. The other hand is on the back of his neck, and two lights later it hasn’t moved.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 5:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — TRUMBULL, COLLECT
body: The east stairwell at ten past five smells of somebody’s microwave popcorn from the lounge upstairs, and the last of the sun comes through the wired glass in one slab and falls across the third step. Jack has the RAZR shut on his knee, because he has been about to call Gina since lunch. Danny’s calls are Wednesdays. It goes off anyway. The little outside screen shows a row of dashes, and a woman’s recorded voice is already talking before he’s all the way open.

*This is a prepaid call from* — and then Danny, fast, into the gap they leave him, “*Danny*” — *an inmate at an Ohio correctional institution. This call is subject to monitoring and recording. To accept, press one.*

He presses one hard enough that the cracked hinge answers. Two girls come down the stairs with a laundry basket between them, arguing about a roommate’s comforter, and he pulls his feet in; the basket goes by at the height of his ear and the argument goes with it, around the turn.
“Professor.” Behind the voice a television is going at full volume and a man is laughing at it, and somewhere a steel door closes on something. “It’s after eight. They’re being generous.”
“Happy birthday, Dan.”
“Again. It’s my day. I get an encore.”
“Happy birthday.”
“Twenty-three.” Danny tries it on, like a coat that might be big in the shoulders. “Reggie says that’s when you start counting in knees.”
“Did they sing?”

“At count. The whole tier, in about four keys, and one guy on harmony nobody asked for. Then Dunleavy came down with the clipboard and said *happy birthday, Costigan* without looking up. Like a citation.” A chair scrapes on his end. “Patty melt for supper and a pudding cup. Reggie ate the pudding. He says it’s tradition.”

body.text: “So,” Danny says. “The nun.”

“Her name’s Skye.”

“I know her name. I asked the chaplain about Catherines. He says there’s four.” A pause for the television. “He says the one from Siena yelled at popes.”

“That’s her.”

“That’s what I told him.”

body: “What are you reading?” Jack says.
“The O’Connor you sent. The guy who preaches off the hood of his car, the church with no Jesus in it. Won’t anybody listen to him.” A breath. “I like him. He’s got a car.”
“*Wise Blood.*”
“That’s the one.”
“Skye booked a show,” Jack says. “Outside Santa Fe. She leaves Saturday.”
“What’s she play?”
“A sheriff’s daughter. She isn’t nice to anybody.”

“Good for her. I’d watch that one.” Danny’s voice moves off the mouthpiece and comes back. “Ma’s bringing the candle the fourteenth. Same as the last two Februaries. It gets as far as the lobby and sits in a bag with my number on it till she goes home.” He says it like the weather. “They won’t let it through. Fire.”
Somewhere behind him a man yells something with *rich one* in it. “Reggie wants to know is the rich one still rich.”
“Tell Reggie more so.”
“He says that’s all he wanted to know. Eleven minutes, Professor. Give me something.”
So Jack gives him the one thing he has. “Theo asked me to New Orleans. For the Super Bowl. He printed six tickets off the lab printer, and one of them says COSTIGAN.”
“The rich one printed you a ticket.”
“He says it’s refundable.”
“Nothing’s refundable. Ask Pop about the Browns.” The television gets louder and then somebody turns it down. “The rich one *asked* you something? He don’t ask. He offers.”
“First time.”
“So you told a guy who never asks no. How’d he take it?”
“He folded the placemat in thirds and put it in his jacket. Then he paid for both of us.”
“Huh,” Danny says. And then: “The veil girl’s town.”
“I’m not going.”
“You ain’t going ’cause of the TV one, or ’cause of the veil girl?”
Down the shaft a door bangs and somebody yells a name that isn’t his.
“Neither.”
“That’s two,” Danny says.
“I’m not saying two.”
“I’m saying two. You’re not saying anything.” On his end a man says *Costigan, you done?* and Danny says *two minutes* with a hand over the mouthpiece that doesn’t cover it.
“Her letter’s gone soft,” he says. “I read it so much. Reggie says that’s a sign. She wrote my number big at the top. Bigger than you do.”
“I did the envelope.”
“I know your hand, Professor. She put the stamp on straight.” The man says *Costigan* again, closer, and Danny drops his voice. “I wrote the TV one back. Last week. Don’t read it.”
“It isn’t addressed to me.”
“It’s addressed to her. You carry it. You don’t read it over her shoulder, and you don’t do the face.”

choices.text: Tell him what you sang at a red light today, for his birthday.
choices.key: On his twenty-third birthday you told Danny what you sang at a red light that afternoon. He laughed till the CO looked over.
response: “State Street. The light at Carrillo. Top down.” He gives him the title straight, “Birthday Sex,” and then, because it’s his birthday, “All of it, Dan. For you.”

For two seconds there is only the dayroom on the line: the television, a chair. Then it starts somewhere under Danny’s ribs and comes up through the phone, the big one, and a voice that isn’t Danny’s says *Costigan, phone’s for talking*, and Danny says, “It *is* talking, sir, it’s my *birthday*,” and goes under again.
“*Professor.*” He is wiping his eyes; Jack can hear it. “At a red light. Who did the high part?”
“She did.”
“And you?”
“The rest. Committed. Terrible.”
“That’s the only way to do it.” A breath. “Anybody see?”
“A girl in the next lane. She had a Flip.”
“A *Flip*.” The laugh comes down a step at a time. “Happy birthday to *me*.”

choices.text: “I lit you a candle. Mary side.”
response: “Noon Mass,” Jack says. “They gave out tapers. I got wax on the Carhartt.”
“On my jacket.”
“It’ll come out.”

“With a hot iron and a paper bag. Ask Ma.” The dayroom noise drops, as if Danny has turned his back on it. “Nonna’s got mine in the drawer with the matches. For weather. I’m a weather candle.” A breath. “You lit me one. Mary side. Which Mary.”
“There’s one Mary, Danny.”
“Not in Ma’s kitch—”
Jack says *Danny?* to the dial tone anyway.

choices.text: “Phil saw his shadow. Six more weeks of you.”
response: “Pop take it personal?”
“He took it personally, Dan. Said so to Ma’s phone, from the truck.”

“That’s Pop.” Danny laughs without much sound, a breath through the nose that Jack knows from the cab of a Silverado. “Phil’s got no pull in here, Professor. It’s been six more weeks since I got here.” He lets Jack have that one.
Behind him somebody calls time. “Happy birthday to me,” Danny says, and hangs up on himself.

s06a.slug: TUESDAY · 8:55 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — LOST
body: The recap has a few minutes left in it when Jack gets the glass door open, and the Fishbowl is lit blue and moving: a man in a ruined shirt running down a beach, a hatch, another hatch. Doug has unrolled the poster board across the coffee table and pinned its four corners with the Fishbowl’s mugs, and he kneels over it on the carpet with an orange marker in each hand. His phone sits in a manila envelope on Priya’s table by the door, marked EAST COAST, where he surrendered it at six. Kevin’s spot against the radiator, where he reads orgo through anything, is just a radiator tonight.

Margot takes her feet off the loveseat as Jack comes in. “Sit,” she says. “I’m studying who sits where since Wednesday. It’s a small sample.” The loveseat’s near arm touches the end of the far couch. He sits.
“Father Jack,” Theo calls from the far couch, with the fountain pen raised in salute. “You’ve chosen the island.”
“I came for the key.”
“Wise. Pruitt’s is the only honest document in the building.” It is a good bit, delivered a notch above its usual volume, and Jack laughs at it anyway, because it is a good bit.
“Okay,” Doug says. “*Okay.* New theory. It’s purgatory.”
“That’s the old theory.”
“It’s the old theory with a *key*. They keep saying it’s not purgatory, and that’s how you know.”
“Doug. Purgatory is for the saved. Everybody on that island is getting worse.”
“It’s *symbolic*.”
“Purgatory doesn’t have a polar bear.”

Doug takes this in. He uncaps the orange, writes *BEAR??* in the corner of the chart, and underlines it. “Also, dude,” he says over his shoulder, “the other Jack’s on tonight. The doctor. He’s got your hair.”
“He doesn’t.”
“He’s got the *worry*.”

“I have a thesis,” Margot says from the armchair. Her notebook is open on one knee. “The island is a Protestant work ethic. No one on it is permitted to simply *rest*. They build a hatch, or they press a button in the hatch, or they are punished for not pressing the button. It is Calvin with a polar bear.”
“Dude, you can’t put that on the key.”
“I wouldn’t dream of it.”

On the far arm of the couch Yusuf has *Nine Stories* open and the lid on his pen, his back half turned to the screen. “Yusuf, dude, come look at the key,” Doug says. “I’m listening,” Yusuf says. “It’s *visual*.” “I’ll hear about it.” He turns a page. “It sounds like a bridge being built by the people crossing it.”
At her table Priya has the Handbook open and does not look up from it. “Oceanic 815 went down on the twenty-second of September, 2004,” she says. “You have 2005.”
“It’s a theory,” Doug says.
“It’s a calendar.” Priya turns a page and goes on not watching.

The recap ends to a cheer that she quells with one look, and the program begins. On the far couch Theo has the blazer on and the fountain pen in its pocket, and a yellow legal pad lies face down on the cushion between him and Laney, who sits cross-legged in the Pi Lam sweatshirt with Priya’s Pyrex bowl of popcorn in her lap. They have been negotiating at a stage whisper, audible at the glass, since before Jack came in.
“A sorbet,” Theo is saying, “is a palate cleanser. A birthday is not a palate.”
“I’m fixin’ to turn nineteen, Theodore, and I want it to look like I meant to. And a harpist. A girl gets one birthday.”
“Two, in Dallas. It’s a recurring franchise.”
“Once. Everything after is a rerun.”
“Then the cart *and* the harpist. A cart says *intention*. A harp says *intention with a draft*.”
“And our next contestant,” Laney says, as a plane shudders over the ocean, “is a man in a window seat who doesn’t know it yet.”

Laney goes on at Theo about napkins out of the side of her mouth and, with her eyes on him, holds the bowl out sideways at the end of her arm to whoever is on that side. Jack, who is on that side, takes a handful. “Thanks.”
She looks round. She sees whose hand is in the bowl, and the bowl comes back against her sweatshirt, and stays there.
“Bless your heart,” Laney says, and the temperature of it drops at *heart*. She gives the screen her profile. “What was I saying?”
“Harp,” Theo says, gently.

On the arm of the couch Theo’s iPhone lights up with a text that begins MSY and a time. His hand comes down over it without his eyes leaving the television, and turns it over, and he goes on with the sorbet.

At the first break Priya starts a kitchen timer at ninety seconds, per the Handbook, for facilities, and nobody moves. Doug sidles over on his knees with the marker still in his fist and lowers his voice to what he believes is a whisper. “Dude. It’s like a custody thing. You get the Fishbowl Tuesdays.”

Jack eats his popcorn. In his pocket the RAZR stays quiet; the sheriff will keep till tomorrow. On the screen the commercials end and a plane comes down out of weather and lands. On this program, that’s news.

s06b.slug: TUESDAY · 8:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE SIDES
body: Every light in her room is on — the lamp, the overhead, the string of Christmas bulbs still tacked over the window — and her iPod is going in its little speaker on the floor by the mattress, the record she’s played since the day it came out. On the mattress is everything she owns that might be warm, in three piles and a fourth pile that’s only socks. In the middle of it sits one suitcase, open, with the look of a suitcase that has just been shown the piles. The coat from State Street hangs on the closet door on the one wooden hanger she owns.

“I said I was bad at it,” Skye says. She’s on her knees in the socks, in leggings and a T-shirt from a 10K she didn’t run, with a pencil stuck through her hair. “I’ve been doing this an hour. So far I’ve packed a hair dryer.”
“They have hair dryers in New Mexico.”
“They have *motels* in New Mexico. I’ve seen pictures.” She holds up a sweater, looks at it, throws it on the third pile. “The pages are on the pillow. You’re the sheriff.”

The pages are on the pillow: her first week, three-hole-punched, folded the long way and gone soft at the fold, DELL down the left margin over and over like a fence, her pencil in every gap. He picks up four of them.
“I’ve never been a sheriff.”
“You’ve never been a lot of things. Read the capitals that say HARLAN. Don’t act. If you act I’ll have to be nice to you.”
He reads the first HARLAN in his own voice, Glenwood Avenue flat. “*Where were you.*”
“No,” Skye says. “He’s fifty. He has a gun he’s never pointed at anybody. He’s been up since yesterday. Do your dad.”

So he does Frank: Frank Costigan at the kitchen door after midnight with the truck keys still in his hand, finding the Silverado a quarter tank lighter than he left it. Low, tired, no question mark on anything.
“*Where were you.*”
And she’s gone. Not far — she’s right there on the mattress, rolling a pair of socks into a ball — but the girl rolling the socks isn’t anybody he’s met. She doesn’t look up. “Out.”
“*Out where.*”
“Out where you can’t find me.” She drops the socks in the suitcase without looking where they land. “Turns out that’s most places.”

He reads the next HARLAN and she’s over the top of it before he’s halfway, and her eyes come up to him for the first time, and they’ve already decided what he is. She’s dropped her voice half an octave and sped it up, and every word is bored of him, and the back of his neck goes hot.
“*Your mother —*”

“Don’t.” She pulls a sweater off the second pile and folds it perfectly, the first thing she’s folded all night, and lays it in. “You want to talk about Mom, put it in the log, Sheriff. You put everybody else in the log.” She smooths the sweater down. “You found a dead man in an arroyo last spring in forty minutes. In the dark. With one flashlight.” She looks up. “Think about how long you’ve been standing in that door.”
Jack loses his place. It isn’t acting; he can’t find the line. The next HARLAN is somewhere under his thumb, and there’s a girl on the mattress who would let him stand in a doorway till he died.
Then she pulls the pencil out of her hair and her hair comes down, and it’s Skye, cross-legged in a pile of socks, looking at him over the suitcase with her eyebrows up.
“Was that too much?”
“I want to apologize to the horse.”
She lies back in the socks with the pages on her chest. “*Good*,” she tells the ceiling.
“She’s not mean,” she says, from the socks. “Everybody’s going to say she’s mean. She’s *busy*. Every single thing she says in that kitchen is so he won’t get to the next question.”
“What’s the next question?”

“Who she was with.” She points the pencil straight up. “It isn’t in the pages. Nobody told me. I decided. You have to decide, or you’re just saying the words louder.” She rolls her head on the socks to look at him. “She was with a boy her father put in the back of his car last year. She likes the boy. She knows exactly what her father would do if he knew, and she’s right. So she makes it about her mother, because he’ll let her win anything if it’s about her mother.”
“Augustine stole pears,” Jack says. “Off a tree, with his friends, at sixteen. He didn’t even want them. They threw them to the pigs. He says he did it for nothing — for the wrong of it.”

“He says that. He also says he wouldn’t have done it alone.” She sits up. “You told me that part yourself. He had people watching. People don’t do anything for nothing, Youngstown. He just didn’t like who he was showing off for.”
It’s a better reading than the one he wrote a paper on in eleventh grade, and he tells her so. She writes *PEARS* in the margin of page three and underlines it.
The song on the floor ends and the next one starts. She’s quiet through the first of it, the pages on her knees, her thumb going down the margin from one DELL to the next.
“I don’t know who I am when I’m not the nice one,” she says.
“You’re the one who sang that song at a red light on State Street.”
“That’s not a character.”
“No.”
She sets the pages face down on the suitcase lid and holds out both hands for the socks.

He packs the rest Ma’s way, for a week at the lake: everything rolled tight and stood on end, shoes in the corners stuffed with socks, the hair dryer out. It all goes in, all four piles, with room left over. Skye watches from the pillow with her chin on her knees and her eyes on his hands. The coat she keeps out. She’s wearing it on the plane.

At the front door she kisses him in it, over the 10K shirt, with the big collar turned up around her ears because, she says, she wants to know what it’s like to be cold in it, and it’s fifty-five degrees on the porch. Down the bluff stairs the surf is loud.
“Goodnight, Sheriff.”
“Goodnight, Dell.”
“No,” Skye says, with her hand on the door. “The other one.”
“Goodnight, Misfit.”
She pulls the collar up over her mouth and holds the door till he’s down the steps.

s08.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — ST. BLAISE
body: St. Blaise gets the crowd the 12:10 can’t. Half the pews that sat through the Mass stay for the blessing and the rest come in from the courtyard with their sandwiches, and the line goes up the center aisle in two files: Father Osei’s on the left, the deacon’s on the right. The candles are two to a bundle, crossed and tied in red ribbon. They’re yesterday’s, blessed at the card table with the rest. Under the A-frame the air is warm with a hundred people who have not yet gone back to work.

Blaise was a bishop in Armenia who talked a fishbone out of a boy’s throat, and was martyred for the rest of it with iron wool combs, a detail the third grade at St. Brigid’s never spared anybody. He is the patron of throats and wool-combers. Today the Church lines up its throats in front of him, and Jack is in the line with the most-watched throat in Santa Barbara County. The Church, he has always said, has terrific timing. He has not always meant it as a compliment.

He picked Osei’s file without deciding to, and has had the length of the aisle to wonder what that says about him. Peter Haddad, two ahead, tells Osei his throat is fine, thank you, at a volume that suggests otherwise. “A fine throat is the one in most danger, Peter,” Osei says, and lifts the candles. “It is the healthy ones that go and say things.” Tyler Brandt, ahead of Peter, turns around and gives Jack two thumbs up, and then, to be sure Jack has the reference, mouths *Brother?* with the question mark in it.

In the front pew, where she can see every face on its way up the aisle, Mrs. Fitch sits with her purse on her knees and her grandson beside her, thirteen, in a Giants cap, holding an iPod Touch against his chest like a hymnal. When Jack comes level with the pew the boy looks up at him with the plain, unguarded awe of a child meeting an actual Giant. “Seagull,” he whispers, with deep respect. Mrs. Fitch moves one hand from the iPod to the back of his neck without turning her head. Then she turns it, to Jack. It is a long look. It starts at his face and stays there, and when it’s finished she faces front again. There is no table. There are no lemon bars. Lemon bars are Sunday.
“You have a really nice voice, Jack.”
Becca is one step behind him in the line, in her buttoned coat, with her hands folded.
“You’ve seen it.”
“Kenzie showed me in the courtyard. Twice.” She considers. “The middle part is really warm.”
“Thank you, Becca.”
“You’re welcome. Kenzie says she could take the high part for you, next time. She says that isn’t a criticism.”
“Tell her thank you.”

Lena is in the other line, the deacon’s, on the Mary side. When the candles come away from her throat she crosses herself and goes out the side door into the courtyard while there are still a dozen people ahead of him.

Then it’s his turn. Osei lifts the crossed candles to his throat, one in each hand, and Jack raises his chin into the scratch he’s had since a red light on State Street. The wax is cold under his jaw, and the knot of the red ribbon rests in the hollow of his collar like a coin.

“Through the intercession of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, may God deliver you from every disease of the throat and from every other illness: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
Osei’s eyes are on him for the length of the blessing, and they stay on him when the candles come away. He sets one hand on Jack’s shoulder. Behind them the deacon’s file has already moved up two.
“Eight o’clock,” he says, low, for Jack alone.

s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:30 PM · THE COMMONS LAWN — GLENWOOD
body: By half past four the Commons lawn has decided it’s June. Towels, a boy on a slackline strung between two eucalyptus, a dog standing guard over a Frisbee that isn’t his; the sprinklers came on at four and nobody on the grass has agreed to notice. Jack sits against a trunk with the wet coming up through his jeans from the last pass of the water and *Brideshead Revisited* open on his knee to a page he has been on since three.
The RAZR buzzes on the grass beside him. The little outside screen says GLENWOOD, on a Wednesday. Ma calls on Sundays.

“Jackie.” She doesn’t say hello or ask if he ate. Behind her something is on a back burner, the lid ticking in its seat. “I made the soup first. I wanted to be a person who made the soup first.” A cupboard shuts. “Rita Pallante’s youngest has a telephone.”

His stomach drops. He is nine again, in the plastic chair outside the St. Brigid’s office, with Ma on the other side of the glass pretending not to know him. The dog has abandoned the Frisbee and come to sit on his shoe, interested. He has an answer ready, shaped like *it’s a pop song, Ma*, and it doesn’t get out.

“He showed Rita,” she says. “In the church lot. Then Rita showed the kitchen.” The parish kitchen, where the Wednesday ladies fold the fish-fry flyers: ten pairs of reading glasses around one phone the size of a cookie. “I’m told it was very quiet. Then Pat DeLuca asked was it a hymn. Father Dom was in the room. He watched to the end. He said *she has a good voice* and went to see about the boiler.”
From the kitchen table, flat, nowhere near the phone, his father says, “I told her it’s about a birthday.”
“Frank.”
“It’s about a birthday.”
“Your father says it’s about a birthday,” Ma says into the phone. “He’s said it to Rita, and to Rita’s machine, and to the mailman, who didn’t ask.”

body.text: “She knelt, you told me. Sunday.” She doesn’t finish it. The kitchen fills in behind her: a spoon on the rim of a pot, a chair, the dryer buzzing down the cellar stairs.

body: In the front room Nonna is in the middle of a decade, audible through two doors, and at the end of every Hail Mary the name goes in just ahead of the *Amen*. *Maria Caterina.*
“She watched it,” Ma says. “Gina held her phone up to the chair. Twice. She says the girl sings like an angel.” A pause. “Jackie. She doesn’t speak English.”
“Then how does she —”
“She knows a voice.”

There’s a scuffle, and the receiver comes back hot and small: Gina, who has run for it. “Jack. *Jack.* Okay, I’m telling you before Ma does, so don’t say I didn’t. Ryan Pallante called the *house*. To apologize for his mother. Ma said *tell Rita thank you*, and Pop took the phone and said *tell your mother I said hello*, and Ryan said *yes, sir* like nine times. I could hear him sweating through the cord.”
“Pop said hello?”
“Like a hello with a tire iron in it.”

body.text: “And Danny called at four, it’s his Wednesday, and I was *so* ready, I said *Danny, you’re not going to believe*, and he said *I KNOW, HE TOLD ME YESTERDAY*, and Ma put her hand over her eyes.”
body.else: “And I told Danny on his call, and he laughed till the CO came over. Again.”

body: Gina’s voice goes away from the phone and comes back smaller. “Rosie wants you.”
“Jack. Is the crab in it?”
“Not this one, Ro.”
“Then why is everybody so upset?”
Before he can find an answer for an eight-year-old, Ma has the phone: “Rosie. Bath.”
“Gina. *Upstairs.*” Feet on the stairs, and a door.
“Your father wants a word,” Ma says, and the line fills with his breathing, close, the breathing from the cab of the Silverado.
“Pop.”
“That’s a Saab.”
“It’s hers, Pop.”
“GM had half of Saab in ninety-one.” A chair creaks. “I looked it up. On the Dell.”
“I didn’t know that.”
“Well.” Frank doesn’t say what the *well* is for. “Good car,” he says, and the receiver goes back across the kitchen.
“Is she good to you?”

He thinks of a post on his wall at twelve past six this morning, and Corinne on the phone at five-forty, and what one good song has cost somebody by now. Across the lawn the boy on the slackline comes off, stands there with his arms out, and gets back on.
Jack hasn’t answered when Ma adds, quieter, “It’s Wednesday, Jackie.”

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’ Sunday, after the 8:00 and Trumbull: Father Dom said a prophet’s never welcome at home, and Pop said that’s for sure in the pew. She’d seen the taco picture: *she’s tiny.* Then one question — did I go up today. I said yes. She said good. Candlemas, from the vestibule: Danny’s twenty-three. Two letters beats one card. Wednesday she called about the song. Rita Pallante’s youngest showed Rita, and Rita showed the parish kitchen. Pop told her it’s about a birthday. She asked me one thing: is she good to me. Then: it’s Wednesday, Jackie.

choices.text: “She’s good to me, Ma.”
choices.key: Ma called about the song. She asked one thing — is she good to you. You told her she is.
response: “Good.” A pause the length of the kitchen. “Good.” And then, the first normal thing she has said since hello: “Eat something real tonight. Not the cafeteria.”
“Yes, Ma.”
Far off, from the table, not to the phone: “Tell him the rodent was wrong. It’s sunny.”

choices.text: “It was stupid, and it was the happiest I’ve been all year.”
choices.key: Ma called about the song. You told her it was stupid, and the happiest you’ve been all year.
response: Ma doesn’t answer. The lid ticks, and the dryer down the cellar stairs runs out its cycle with a buzz.
“I could see that,” she says at last. “I could see it from here. That’s what worries me.”
Through the wall the beads stop, and then they go on.

choices.text: “I’m sorry, Ma.”
choices.key: Ma called about the song. You told her you were sorry. She told you not to be sorry to her — you know who to be sorry to.
response: “Don’t be sorry to me, Jackie.” It comes with no edge on it at all. “You know who to be sorry to.”
The lid lifts on its own steam. “The pot,” Ma says, and hangs up on the sound of it.

body: The hall window has gone from dusk to nothing by the time Jack gets back to 412, and he has eaten something at the Commons that he is already negotiating with. The Carhartt is on its hook inside, where it has hung since morning, and the hill to St. Brendan’s is not warm at night. He gets the door open on his own room and on Laney’s voice, low and fast and pitched for a room with the door shut:
“— she’d *decided*, Theodore, she’d —”
It stops where it is.

412 has more people in it than it has chairs, and Hollis presides over them from his teacup on the nightstand. Laney is cross-legged on Theo’s bed in the Pi Lam sweatshirt with a fan of printed pages in one fist, striped at the edges by a printer low on toner, held like a hand she means to lose. Theo stands at the closet door with a green marker uncapped. The double-sided board he bought in October to outline his one-act, and which Jack has been forbidden to touch since the Sharpie, hangs there on a brass swivel, turned to its blank face, though where the two faces meet at the frame a stroke of marker has gone around the corner: the bottom curve of a capital *B*. Theo takes a half step sideways, into the way of it. Kevin sits against the radiator in pajama pants printed with the periodic table and a Marisol quarter-zip zipped to the chin, so that the top half of him is attending a meeting and the bottom half is in bed. Margot has turned Jack’s desk chair around backward and sits in it with her notebook on the chair back and her pen up.
Four faces turn to the door at the same speed, and the printed pages go face-in against Laney’s sweatshirt. Jack stands in his own doorway. It’s a new experience.
“Costigan,” Theo says, a full tone brighter than Theo. “My moral compass. You’ve walked in on the planning of a surprise.”
“For who?”
“My birthday,” Laney says. “It’s a production, fireman.”

“Logline,” Theo says. “A girl of nineteen is given the Bacchus Sunday she deserves, at the Broussards’, by the friends she has sorely tried. It has a harpist. Marguerite, Lafayette, bar mitzvahs, and also a notary, which in this economy is a business model. Forty-one guests, a sorbet cart, provisional, and seating by temperament. Pruitt is a sanguine.”
“She knows about it?”
“I’m being briefed,” Laney says. “I’m very surprised.”
“That’s the trip,” Jack says.
“It’s a birthday that happens to occur inside the trip,” Theo says. “The napkins are not up for discussion.”
“Kev,” Jack says, at the pajama pants. “What’s the birthday?”
“The fourteenth.” Kevin is looking at the carpet, and goes on looking at it. “It’s a Sunday. It’s Valentine’s. She’s very proud of it. I’m here under protest, and I’d like that recorded.”
“That’s my desk,” Jack tells Margot.

“It’s a desk. I’m observing from it.” Margot lowers the pen. “The observer notes that a man has entered his own room and been received as a guest, which is a finding. Don’t mind me. I’m here as an observer. Of the birthday.” She writes something down.
Jack has twenty minutes and a hill. He takes the Carhartt off its hook by the door and gets one arm into it.
“Where to, my moral compass?” Theo says. “‘Out’ is a mood, not a destination.”
“Out.”
“In the Carhartt. In February. Very Ohio. Say one for the harpist.”
“She’s a notary. She can say her own.”
“Happy birthday, Laney,” Jack says, from the door.
“It’s in eleven days.”
“Then early.”
Laney’s smile arrives a beat after the rest of her, and it’s the wrong size.

s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:55 PM · OCEAN ROAD → ST. BRENDAN’S — THE LIGHT IS ON
body: Down from Delgado the streetlights on Ocean Road come one to a block, and between them the dark is the real kind: eucalyptus, somebody’s woodsmoke, the sea off to the right somewhere below the bluffs, louder than it looks. Jack has the Carhartt zipped to the collar. Behind him 412 is full of people planning a birthday eleven days early. Ahead of him the A-frame comes up out of the dark with the olive tree leaning over the courtyard wall, a boat somebody turned over on the hill and forgot to come back for.

At the back of the nave, behind the blue glass, the bulb over the closet door is lit. It’s a forty-watt in a wire cage, the kind Pop has over the garage side door on Glenwood, and it means one thing. *Eight o’clock*, Osei said at noon, with the candles still crossed under Jack’s chin.

He has it ready. He’s had it ready since the wax came away from his throat: the red light on State Street and the song, and what that was and what it wasn’t; Sunday, and the bath, and her bed, and the word *when*, let stand in the dark. He could say all of it on the steps without stopping for breath. He knows what the man on the far side of the linen will want at the end of it, too, because it’s what the sacrament wants at the end of everything, and any second-grader at St. Brigid’s could tell you what it is.

At the foot of the steps a sprinkler hisses across the last of the parish lawn and wets the sidewalk in a half circle and starts back. The courtyard gate has been propped open with a brick. Somebody has thought of everything.

s11a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE BOX
body: The card table inside the doors is bare tonight, no lamp and no binder and no Mrs. Fitch, and the nave is dark to the altar. On the closet door the index card still says KNOCK (GENTLY) in her hand, and under it, on a length of string, somebody has thumbtacked a golf pencil, in case a person needs to write it all down first. He stands in front of it with his hand up. He knocks gently. On the far side the beads stop.
Inside it’s the closet: the kneeler, the linen, the coat hooks from 1962. The vinyl on the kneeler has split at one corner since last week, and a little yellow foam shows under his left knee.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been a week since my last confession.”
“A week.” The chair on the far side takes Osei’s weight. “And five minutes early. My mother used to say that a man who comes early to the house is carrying bad news or good fish. Which is it?”
“Probably both, Father.”
“The news first, then. Fish keeps.”
He starts with the song, because it’s the easy one, and it turns out not to be.

“Tuesday I was in a car with Skye. Her car, top down, at a red light on State Street. A song came on the radio and we sang it to each other. All of it, at the top of our lungs.” The linen moves a little with somebody breathing on the other side of it. “It’s about sex, Father. That’s all it’s about. It isn’t even a little bit about anything else. It’s called —”
“I know what it is called.” A pause of a very particular quality. “Mrs. Fitch’s grandson has very good speakers.”
Jack shuts his eyes. Out in the courtyard the sprinkler comes around and goes away again.

“A girl in the next lane filmed it,” he says. “It’s on the internet. My mother’s parish kitchen has seen it. I didn’t mean anything wrong by it, Father, I’m not going to tell you I did. It was the best two minutes of my week, and I didn’t think about it for one second of them.” He finds the rest where he left it, on the walk down. “I’ve been coming in here since before Christmas about one thing. I keep telling you it matters. And Tuesday I sang it like a joke, at a stoplight, with a medal on, where anybody could see. It makes the thing smaller. For me, and for her, and for every kid with a phone who watched a guy who goes to Mass do it. It makes it easier to laugh at.” He doesn’t make it bigger than that, or smaller. “It’s venial. I know it is. It’s a venial sin with about forty thousand people watching.”

“When I was a houseman at Korle-Bu,” Osei says, “there was a drug we gave for everything. Every cough, every fever, every man who wanted to go home with something in his hand. By the time I left, it worked on nobody.” The beads click once. “Words are like that, Jack. The good ones and the holy ones most of all. Give them out for everything and they will do nothing on the day you need them. And people watch you now, because of her and because of that medal. They learn from the people they watch what is allowed to be funny. Sing in the car. Choose the song.”
“Yes, Father.”
“And the fish.”
“Sunday,” Jack says.

He tells it to the linen in short words. “Sunday I received at the eleven-thirty. She came. She knelt. Sunday night I was at her house. A bath, and then her bed. Everything but the one thing, and further than it’s ever gone.” The foam gives under his knee. “She asked me for the one thing first. Before any of it, at the top of her stairs, straight out. I said no. I said *for now*.” He makes himself say the last of it. “After, she said *when*. I didn’t correct her.” And because it belongs on the kneeler with the rest: “I haven’t gone up since. Not Tuesday, not today.”
On the other side the beads go once around something and stop.
“She knows you are here tonight?”
“She told me to come. She said I have to tell you I won’t do it again.” He hears how it sounds, a girl in a bed explaining the sacrament to him, and says the rest anyway. “She said that’s the rule.”
Behind the linen there is a sound that, anywhere but here, would be a laugh. “She has the catechism right. Half my confirmation class does not.”

“Before Christmas,” Osei says, “you knelt where you are kneeling, and I told you that you were not avoiding the occasion. You were scheduling it.” The chair creaks. “You have improved. Now you have a timetable. Sunday at the altar. Sunday night down the hill. Wednesday up the hill to me, and then down again. I have walked it. It is downhill all the way from my door to hers. You are not avoiding the near occasion, Jack. You are commuting to it.”

Jack’s face is hot in the dark. There’s a joke lining up in him about the bus schedule, he can feel it coming around the corner, and it doesn’t survive the linen. He doesn’t argue either. There’s nothing in it to argue with.

“You may come every Wednesday of your life,” Osei says, more gently. “I will be in this chair for every one of them; that is what the chair is for. But I would like, one Wednesday, to see you come up this hill from somewhere else.”
“I am not asking you to know the future. Men fall. I am asking what you intend.” The voice behind the linen is quiet and not soft at all. “Do you mean to stay out of that bed?”

He has had an answer for every other thing he carried in here. He looks for this one and finds two of them: the one Osei is owed, and the one that’s true. Down the hill there’s a girl with a car coming for her at six on Saturday morning, and tonight he isn’t sure they’re the same answer.

choices.text: *Tell him you mean to — and mean it.*
choices.key: Behind the screen Father Osei asked what you intend. You told him you mean to stay out of that bed, and meant it. He absolved you.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything. St. Blaise: two crossed candles at my throat, and then, for me, eight o’clock. Wednesday night I went in. I told him the song, all of it, and Sunday night. He said I’m not avoiding the near occasion, I’m commuting to it. He didn’t ask me to know the future. He asked what I intend. I told him I intend to stop. He absolved me.

response: “Yes, Father.” It’s out of him before he’s tested it, so he tests it after, on the kneeler, like a step in the dark, and it takes his weight. “I mean to. I mean to stay out of it.”
“Good.” The beads go still. “Then make a good act of contrition.”

He says the one from St. Brigid’s, the one with *Thee* in it, at the speed he learned it at seven. When he comes to *I firmly resolve, with the help of Thy grace*, he doesn’t have to slow down and look for it. It’s right there where it belongs.

On the linen Osei’s hand rises in shadow. “…through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son” — the shadow goes down the linen and across it — “and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“For your penance, a decade. The Presentation. Slowly. The old man in the temple waited; he will not mind waiting for you.” A breath. “Go in peace.”
“Thanks be to God.”

The side door lets him out into the courtyard. The air off the water has turned while he was inside, salt and wet olive leaves and cut grass, and his knee carries the print of the split vinyl into it. Behind him, through the blue glass, the bulb over the closet door is still lit for whoever’s next.
