journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything. St. Blaise: two crossed candles at my throat, and then, for me, eight o’clock. Wednesday night I went in. I told him the song, all of it, and Sunday night. He said I’m not avoiding the near occasion, I’m commuting to it. He didn’t ask me to know the future. He asked what I intend. I told him the truth: I don’t know that I do. He couldn’t absolve me. He blessed me instead. The light’s on Wednesdays, he said. He’ll be there.

response: “I don’t know, Father.” He shifts on the kneeler. “I want to say yes. I walked down here to say yes. I don’t know that I mean it.”
It goes quiet through the linen, quiet enough that he hears a car go by on Ocean Road and take its radio with it down the hill.
“Then I can’t give you absolution tonight.” Osei’s voice hasn’t changed at all. “Not because I don’t want to. It isn’t mine to give to a man who hasn’t decided to put the thing down.”
“I know.”

“I know you know.” The chair creaks. “That is why you came. A man who didn’t know would have said yes and gone home light.” Something moves behind the linen. “You may have a blessing. Anyone may have a blessing. I have given one to a deaf dog, and he held still for it.” The shadow of the hand. “May almighty God bless you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“Come back when you can say it. I’ll be here. The light is on Wednesdays.”

body: He doesn’t go up the steps.

From the sidewalk the bulb shows through the blue glass at the back of the nave, small and yellow, one caged light over one door in a dark church. The sprinkler comes around and wets his shoes and goes back. The bulb is still on, and Jack is still on the sidewalk.

He could get through every word of it, with the beads going on the far side. It’s the last thing Osei would ask him that he can’t get past: the one everything else in there hangs on, the line he’s been saying since he was seven, and Jack would have to answer it through a piece of linen to a man he respects.

He knows what he’d say. He’d say yes, because yes is the answer that goes there, and Osei would take it, because a priest takes what you hand him through the screen. And Jack would walk out light and down the hill carrying a yes he never checked. He has said a lot of easy things to a lot of people. He isn’t going to say one through that linen.
A man in a bike helmet comes up Ocean Road on a ten-speed and locks it to the handrail, and stops with one foot on the bottom step when he sees Jack standing there. “You in line?”
“No,” Jack says. “Go ahead.”
The man takes the steps two at a time with the helmet still on, and the door lets him into the dark and closes. The bulb stays lit for the helmet.

Jack puts his hands in the pockets of the Carhartt and walks on, downhill, past the courtyard wall and the olive tree and the end of the parish lawn, where the sidewalk goes dry. At the bottom of Ocean Road the porch light is on at Sol’s, and upstairs, in her window, the Christmas bulbs she never took down are lit end to end. He says a Hail Mary on the way down to them, the kind he says at a crosswalk, fast, under his breath. It’s the one thing he’s sure he can say tonight and mean all of it.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:15 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE SUITCASE
body: Sol’s house is quiet for once. Tomás is out and his stereo is off, and the only thing talking downstairs is the old refrigerator in the kitchen, to itself. Upstairs her door is open and the lamp is on. The suitcase lies open on the floor with its contents climbing back out of it a sweater at a time. A gray sweatshirt hangs over the back of the desk chair. The pages for *Caliche* are spread across the mattress, soft at the fold, her pencil in every margin.
Skye is sitting in the middle of them in the coat from State Street, buttoned to the chin, the big collar up around her ears. “I’m breaking it in,” she says. “It has to know me by Saturday.”

body.text: “Did you tell him?” she says, before he has the Carhartt off.
“Yes.”
“That you won’t.”
“Yes.”

She nods. She looks at his face for a long time, long enough that he can feel it on his skin, and she doesn’t try anything. She gathers the pages off the mattress, knocks them square on her knee, sets them on the suitcase lid, and pats the place where they were. When he lies down she puts her head on his shoulder, coat and all, and folds her hands on his chest where he can see them, and keeps them there.
“I’m not going to make it hard for you,” she says into his shoulder. “Whatever you told him. I wanted you to know that tonight.”

He tells her from the doorway, with the Carhartt still on. Osei asked him what he meant to do, and Jack didn’t know, and said so, and a priest can’t give it to a man who doesn’t know. He got a blessing instead.
She looks up at him from the pages. “Because of me.”
“Because of me,” he says, and touches his own chest, so there’s no mistaking which.

She gets up off the mattress and stands in front of him in the coat, close, and doesn’t touch him. “I cost you that,” she says. “Tonight. Don’t tell me I didn’t. I was in there with you. I’m in there every Wednesday.” She breathes in through her nose and lets it out. “Go back Saturday. I’ll be on a plane. Nothing will be in the way.”
He tells her from the doorway, before she can ask. He got as far as the steps.
“You didn’t go.”
“No.”
“Because you couldn’t say the last part.”
She looks down at the pages in her lap. Down the bluff the surf comes in and goes out again.
“I told you I’m not mad at it,” she says.
He waits.
“I’m a little mad at it.” She doesn’t take it back. She lets him have it. It’s fair.

body: Since breakfast, since Theo turned the laptop around, there’s been an apology in him with nowhere to go. He sits on the edge of the mattress with his elbows on his knees and lets it out.

“I’m sorry,” he says. “About the video. About Cassidy, and the network’s concern, and Corinne on the phone before dawn saying *unfortunate* four times. Your mother at six in the morning.” She opens her mouth and he keeps going. “I’m the one who knew every word. You’ve got a show that pays for a house, and I sang you onto a gossip blog at a red light because I wasn’t thinking about anything but —”

She takes his face in both hands. Her palms are warm from the coat’s pockets. She kisses him slow, and then not slow at all, hard, holding his head exactly where she wants it, the sheepskin collar against his jaw and her knees on either side of his on the edge of the mattress, until there is nothing left in him that was going to finish that sentence. When she lets his mouth go she keeps his face.
“Don’t you ever,” she says, with her forehead nearly on his, “apologize to me for making me happy. Not once. Not as a bit. I won’t have it in the house.”
“Okay.”
“Say it back.”
“I won’t apologize for making you happy.”

“Good.” She pats his cheek twice and sits back on her heels. “Corinne called back tonight to tell me my post was *off-message*. She thinks *the clean version* was about the song. Like I was asking you to learn the radio edit.” She points a finger at his chest. “I wrote it about *you*, Youngstown. You’re the clean version.”
“And the network?”

“The network calls it *the incident*.” She says it like the name of a yacht. “I’ve never been an incident. Cassidy’s never even been a misunderstanding. Three seasons, and the worst thing she ever did was a C in chemistry, and she cried about it for a whole episode.” She pulls the collar up over her chin and looks at him over it. “Dell Harlan would’ve sung the dirty version louder. And then she’d have keyed the Camry.”
“So that’s where you keep it.”
“Keep what?”
“The mean. You asked me Tuesday where you keep it.”
She thinks about that with her chin in the sheepskin. “At red lights,” she says. “Apparently.” Her face is pleased about it.

“My mother wants me to do a sit-down,” she says. “One magazine. Soft lighting. I talk about my faith journey.” She does Debbie for half a line, sweet as a pie case: “*Tears optional, baby.*” Back to herself: “I told her I’m going to New Mexico to be mean to a horse.”
She leans across him to the windowsill, gets her iPhone, and sets the alarm for Saturday, 4:45, three days early, and turns the screen around to show him. “So I believe it.”
She lies back on the mattress in the coat with the phone on her stomach, and holds out one hand to him without looking, palm up, like he’s the one with her pencil. “Stay till I’m asleep.”

choices.text: *Stay till she’s asleep. Then walk home.*
response: He stretches out beside her with his shoes still on. She takes the pages back off the suitcase and reads Dell at the ceiling under her breath, and when she elbows him he does HARLAN, low, out of the margin she points at. She’s asleep inside ten minutes, the pages rising and falling on her chest, halfway through telling her father where she wasn’t.

He slides the script out from under her hand and squares it on the suitcase. He turns off the lamp. In the dark the Christmas bulbs over the window are the only light left in the room, and the surf comes up the bluff and in at the open window, louder with the lamp off.

choices.text: *Tell her a bedtime story about the rodent. Then walk home.*
response: “Once upon a time,” he says, in Frank’s voice, “there was a rodent.”
She turns her head on the pillow. “Oh, good.”

So he gives her Phil of Punxsutawney: a groundhog with a union card, works one day a year, full benefits, dental, a pension the size of a Buick. Lives in a heated burrow the taxpayers of Pennsylvania built him. Has had it in for the state of Ohio since 1953 on account of a remark about his weight. This morning he comes out, in front of a crowd and a tuba, looks down, sees his shadow, and sentences everybody between Pittsburgh and Toledo to six more weeks out of spite.
“What happens to Ohio?” she says, mostly into the collar.
“Ohio files a grievance. And a man in a kitchen in Youngstown puts down his coffee, looks at the TV, and takes it personally, in silence, for six weeks.”
She’s asleep before Ohio gets an answer, collar up to her eyes, the phone sliding off her stomach onto the sheet.

choices.text: *Kiss her at the door and go home while it’s still a kiss.*
response: He takes the hand and pulls her up off the mattress instead, pages and all, and walks her down the stairs to the front door with the coat still buttoned to her chin. On the porch the air off the water is wet and smells of kelp. She kisses him there, under Sol’s porch light, and he kisses her back, and steps down onto the walk while it’s still a kiss.
“Coward,” she says from the doorway, fondly.
“Yes.”

She doesn’t go in. She stands on the porch in the coat with the collar up and her hands in its pockets, and when he looks back from the corner of Del Playa she is still there, being cold in it on purpose.

s13.slug: THURSDAY · 8:30 AM · ANACAPA COMMONS — HOUR FOUR, REPORTED

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Tuesday night he drove Clare to her grandfather’s in Santa Maria to get her violin’s bridge fixed. Hour four was the drive home. He tried what I told him. He said he wanted the drive to be shorter. She fell asleep at Buellton and he drove the rest with the radio off. Thursday he told me somebody asked him to ask me to New Orleans, that he wasn’t going to, and that who asked isn’t his to say. His grandmother wants him at Tết in New Orleans East.

body: On the Louisiana table’s butcher paper somebody has written THREE DAYS in gold marker, and somebody else, in a different hand, has underlined it, and a third has put a fleur-de-lis on the underline. The Commons windows are white to the glass, and the tubes are on at half past eight as if it were November.

Kevin is at the window table with a bowl of oatmeal he is eating in measured quarters, and the corner of an index card shows over the pocket of his shirt. He touches it once as Jack sits, to be sure it’s still there.
“Disclosure first,” he says, before Jack has set down his tray. “Then the report. I like the conflicts out of the way.”
“What conflicts?”
“I was asked to ask you to come to New Orleans.” He says it to the exact middle of Jack’s tray. “I’m not going to. I’m telling you I was asked.”
“By who?”
“That part’s not mine.”
“Theo?”
“That part’s not mine.”
“Kev.”
“It’s a very small part,” Kevin says, “and it’s not mine.”
“Then tell whoever it is no.”

“I don’t carry messages. I do disclosures.” Kevin eats a quarter. “A disclosure goes one way. That’s what makes it one. Your face said no on *New*, by the way. Before *Orleans*. I’m not criticizing. I’m charting it.”
“It’s not a hard question, Kev.”
“It’s the easiest question in the world,” Kevin says, “when you’re already out the door.” The team-captain smile arrives at once, and he pushes the napkins across to Jack.

He goes on in the same sunny voice. He is going himself, as Theo said, and his reasons are Vietnamese. Bà Nội called Sunday and again last night. There is a parish in New Orleans East, Mary Queen of Vietnam, and Tết is the fourteenth, a Sunday: a lion dance, a great many aunts, and a priest who has been told about him. “She said, and I’m translating, *If you are in that city on Tết and you are not at that church, you are not my grandson, and I will have to tell your mother.*” He considers it. “It was the last part that worked. And the fifteenth is my birthday. Laney’s is the fourteenth. Valentine’s. I’m the hangover of a holiday.”
“Presidents’ Day.”
“Which has never been a point of pride for anyone born on it. It has a mattress sale and no other traditions.”

“Now the report.” He takes the index card out of his pocket and lays it face down by the oatmeal with the pen across it, uncapped. “She asked at the candle box at noon, with a taper in her hand. *Do you have a car and a night?* I said I had an Odyssey and a box of tapers. So Tuesday night I drove Clare to Santa Maria. Her grandfather. The bridge on the Czech violin has been leaning since the Walk, and he will only touch it at night, because he says daytime is for people who can’t hear. Seventy miles in the Odyssey, at sixty-five. Hour one was the drive up. Clare gives directions in mile markers. Hours two and three were his kitchen. He asked was I pre-med, I said yes, and he said *Good. Hands.*, and put mine on the body of the violin while he set the bridge with a pencil and a pocketknife. Then he said something to Clare in Spanish, and she went pink to the ears and said *Abuelo*, in a tone I’ve filed under *do not translate*.” He touches the card. “He sent us home with a dozen tamales in a Cool Whip tub that I’m obligated to return, which makes it, formally, a second encounter. I’ve scheduled it.”
“That’s three hours.”
“Three excellent hours. I didn’t say hour four.” Kevin sits up. “Hour four was the drive home.”

body.text: “I tried your answer. Word for word. I had it on the card.”
body.else: “I tried the thing you said. About the drive.”

body: “And?”
“I tried to want the drive to be longer.” Kevin picks up the pen, and puts it down. “I wanted the drive to be shorter.”
Jack waits for the rest. At the Louisiana table somebody does a *Who dat?* and the waffle line answers it.
“There was a truck,” Kevin says.
“A truck.”

“A flatbed. Hay. Forty-one miles an hour from Buellton to the tunnel.” He looks at the oatmeal. “Clare fell asleep at Buellton. I drove the rest with the radio off so she wouldn’t wake.” A pause. “It was very peaceful,” he says, like a diagnosis.

choices.text: “The truck counts, Kev.”
choices.key: Kevin told you hour four was a drive home from Santa Maria, and he wanted the drive to be shorter. You told him the truck counts.
response: “It was a big truck,” Kevin says. He tries the sentence for weight, and it seems to bear him, and the team-captain smile comes up and holds. “A *lot* of hay.”
“At forty-one miles an hour.”
“At forty-one,” Kevin agrees, warmly, as to a fellow witness. He slides the index card back into his pocket without having written a word on it, and goes back to the oatmeal, in quarters.

choices.text: “What did you want instead?”
choices.key: Kevin told you hour four was a drive home from Santa Maria, and he wanted the drive to be shorter. You asked him what he wanted instead.
response: Kevin doesn’t answer. He looks down at the oatmeal for as long as it takes the Louisiana table to get through a *Who dat?* and the waffle line to answer it.
“Orgo,” he says.
“Okay.”

“There’s a midterm the Wednesday we get back. It’s a good midterm. I’ve arranged to take it late; the professor was very understanding about my grandmother.” He stacks Jack’s tray on his own, and carries both to the belt.

choices.text: “Next time make the brothers drive.”
choices.key: Kevin told you hour four was a drive home from Santa Maria, and he wanted the drive to be shorter. You told him next time make the brothers drive.
response: “There are four of them,” Kevin says. “They’d want to vote.”

The idea of four Dominguez brothers in the Odyssey, conducting a roll call at sixty-five, reaches his face by stages. He turns the index card over, writes *brothers drive* on it in his small careful letters, underlines it, and laughs at himself in the quiet way he laughs when no one is keeping score.

s13a.slug: THURSDAY · 9:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE MAILBOXES — TWO ENVELOPES
body: The mailroom window is a white square this morning, and the bare twigs of the jacaranda outside are dripping on the sill without its having rained. Under Priya’s laminate, PACKAGE SLIPS ARE NOT NOTES TO SELF, last week’s Sharpie *they are now* has picked up an answer in green ballpoint, *they always were*, and somebody has drawn a fleur-de-lis under that, because this week somebody draws one under everything.
412’s box is in the third row, at the height of his belt, and its little brass door sticks, as it always has; he has to put his thumb on the 4 and lift. There’s more in it than a bookstore circular.

On top is a long white envelope addressed in block capitals that climb a little toward the end of every line. They climbed like that across the back of every birthday card his brother ever signed. The stamp in the corner says what it says.

body.title: Envelope, Ohio postmark, a stamp in the corner: INMATE CORRESPONDENCE
body.text:
MISS SKYE CALLENDER
c/o JACK COSTIGAN
DELGADO HALL
MARISOL, CALIFORNIA

DANIEL F. COSTIGAN A555218

body: *Don’t read it*, Danny said on Tuesday, with a CO saying his name behind him. *And don’t do the face.* The flap has been sealed and then taped over by a CO who has already read it and was careful about it. Jack holds it up to the white window and gets nothing for his trouble but lines of capitals showing through the paper backward, mirror writing he could work out if he stood here long enough, and he isn’t going to stand here. He zips it into the inside pocket of the Carhartt.
Under it is a card.

It’s folded once, cream, of a stock heavy enough to stand up on its own, and there’s a fleur-de-lis at the top — not printed, pressed into the paper, so that his thumb finds it before his eyes do. Marisol doesn’t run to paper like this. Somebody’s mother does. On the outside, in pencil, it says *Jack*, and he knows the hand from the margins of half the books on his shelf: the J that starts above the line, the k with a kick in its leg, a pencil kept sharp enough to cut.
At the far end of the wall, past the 300s, the 200s are in the shade, and there’s nobody at 217. He opens it standing up, with his bag still on his shoulder.

body.title: A cream card, a fleur-de-lis pressed at the top
body.text:
Jack —

Theo says you’re not coming. Mémère says that isn’t a thing people say to her. Mama has made up the twins’ room, and Daddy says the Saints have never won one with a Costigan in the house, which is true.

American, Friday, 1:15. There’s a seat.

You’d be welcome.

—L.

body: Which is true. The Saints have never won one with anybody in the house.
Theo’s flight, to the minute. Her mother’s manners, Jack figures: an invitation on the good stock, whether anybody meant it or not.

It’s a question he already answered. He folds it back along its crease and puts it in the *Brideshead* in his back pocket, at Book Three. It’s stiff enough to make a good bookmark. He’ll be able to find his place by feel.

Doug comes in from the lobby in shower shoes, says “Dude,” with some urgency, to the package window, and is handed a box the size of a microwave that says LOGITECH on the side. “Speakers,” he tells Jack, holding it up like a trophy he found. “For the island. Dude, *surround*.” He goes out hugging it.
Jack shuts 412’s little door. It sticks. He lifts, with his thumb on the 4, and it latches.

s14.slug: THURSDAY · 1:00 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — PHIL 109H — THROUGH THE CHAIR
body: The fog has gone off the hill by one, and the wind that took it is working the eucalyptus outside 302, so that at the window end of the long table the light keeps arriving and leaving. At the door end, under the clock, there’s only the fluorescent tube and the radiator. That end is Jack’s.

It is the first time the table has sat since the door on its trestles. Evan is at the door with the roster on its clipboard, clicking his pen at each name. Yusuf has the corner, his Commons coffee with the lid on it, and a ballpoint beside the cup with its cap on too. The two girls from the window side have their *Brideshead*s out, one of them a library copy in a plastic jacket that crackles whenever she turns a page. Caleb, whose account of Hale’s went through Delgado by way of Doug and came out the other end with chairs in it, is sitting so still he could be having his portrait taken in 1890.
At the window end, in the last chair, Lena has her copy squared to the edge of the table with the pencil laid across it. It’s a long table. That’s what it’s for.

Hale comes in at four minutes past with his coat over his arm and the Williams in his back pocket. He has shaved, and missed a place under the jaw, and his eyes are pink at the rims. He takes the roster from Evan without reading it and sits down halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end, and he turns it now, to one end and then the other, taking his time about each.

“I have spent four days in New York being called *my dear man* by a bishop on a stage,” he says. “I find I’m in the mood for intermediaries. I’ve had a bellyful of direct address.” He lays the roster down. “Until I say otherwise, Mr. Costigan and Miss Broussard will address all remarks to the chair.”
Caleb’s hand comes partway up off the table. “Is that —” He looks for the word. “Legal?”

“It’s pedagogy, Mr. Hargrove.” Hale gets up, uncaps a marker and writes on the whiteboard behind him in his tilted capitals, IS JULIA RIGHT TO SEND CHARLES AWAY?, and caps the marker and sits back down. “The chair is me. You will find the chair accurate, impartial and very slightly drunk on the sound of its own voice, which is to say a chair like any other. Miss Broussard. The floor. Address it to me.”
Lena leaves the book shut.

“Yes, Professor,” she says, to Hale. “She’s right, and it’s the only honest thing anybody does in the novel. Everybody in that house is lying to somebody. Charles is lying to his wife. Rex is lying to everyone, professionally. Bridey isn’t lying, but that’s only because nobody has ever asked him a question. Julia looks straight at the one thing she wants most in the world, says exactly what it’s going to cost her, and pays it.” Now she does open the book, to a page she doesn’t have to look for. “She won’t *set up a rival good to God’s*. She doesn’t dress it up as a sacrifice, either — she calls it a bargain, she’s that honest. Lord have mercy, Professor. A woman who knows the price and pays it anyway isn’t a fanatic. She’s the only grown-up in the book.”

Hale turns his head the long way back, past Caleb’s portrait and Yusuf’s capped pen, to the door end. “Miss Broussard says,” he says, “and I am paraphrasing only slightly: *yes, obviously*.” He folds his hands on the roster. “Mr. Costigan. The chair awaits your reply. The chair is not getting any younger.”

It’s easier than he would have thought. A sentence goes down the table to Hale and comes back with Hale’s fingerprints on it, and none of it has to travel the length of the varnish in a straight line. He has had worse arrangements. He has, this month, had nearly all of them.

choices.text: “Professor, she calls it a private bargain. Tell her Charles pays for it and never signed it.”
response: Hale delivers it down the table with both eyebrows. “Mr. Costigan observes that the bargain is private, and the bill has gone to Mr. Ryder.”

“Then tell Mr. Costigan Charles isn’t paying for her bargain, Professor,” Lena says. “He’s being spared. Spared a woman who’d have hated him inside a year for being the thing she put in God’s place — and hated herself worse, and taken it out on the furniture. She’s doing him a kindness he’s too proud to recognize. Men usually are.”

choices.text: “Professor, tell Miss Broussard that Waugh rigs the deck — he hands Julia God and Charles a paintbrush.”
response: “Mr. Costigan,” Hale tells the window end, enjoying himself enormously, “feels the deck is rigged.”
“Tell Mr. Costigan,” Lena says, to Hale, “the paintbrush is the only thing Charles ever loved that didn’t love him back.”
Caleb laughs, and stops, and goes back to sitting for his portrait. It’s a better line than Jack’s. From the door end he can afford to admit that, to himself.

choices.text: “She’s right that it costs Julia. Tell her I’ll give her that.”
response: Hale relays it slowly, with one eyebrow up, and doesn’t improve it.
At the window end there’s a pause, a short one, that Lena doesn’t use for anything. “Tell him thank you,” she says, to Hale.
It’s the only thank-you of the hour, and it goes to the chair. “The chair is moved,” Hale says, drily, “and expects to recover.”

choices.text: “Ask her whether Charles was ever asked what he believed.”
response: Hale asks her, turning the top half of himself toward the window to do it.

“He was asked every day for ten years, Professor,” Lena says. “By every Flyte in that house, at every meal, with the chapel right off the hall. Lady Marchmain asked him. Cordelia asked him. Sebastian asked him just by being Sebastian. And every single time he answered with that face he makes, the one like he’s smelled the sacristy.” She doesn’t wait for Hale. “Asking isn’t the trouble in that book. Answering is.”
Hale turns back to the door end. “Mr. Costigan,” he says, “you’ve been answered.”

s14a.slug: THURSDAY · 1:25 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — A TWITCH UPON THE THREAD
body: Twenty minutes in, the room has learned the rhythm the way a congregation learns a new Mass setting: a line goes down to Hale, Hale turns his head, the line goes on, and every head at the table goes with it, down and back. Yusuf has stopped pretending to read and holds his coffee in both hands, following. Evan has written the date at the top of a fresh page of the roster and nothing under it.
Caleb is the first to crack. “Can *I* talk to her?” he asks Hale. “Like, directly? Is that allowed? For the rest of us?”
“The rule binds the principals, Mr. Hargrove. You may address anybody you like.” Hale doesn’t look round. “I can’t promise anyone will listen. That has always been the case.”

Caleb turns in his chair toward the window end and opens his mouth, and discovers that he has nothing to say to Lena Broussard about *Brideshead Revisited* that he wants to say in this room, today, with Jack Costigan under the clock; and he turns back, and studies the whiteboard as though it might be on the final.
At the window end Lena lifts her pencil off the book.
“Miss Broussard has asked the chair for the floor,” Hale says, “by raising a pencil, which the chair has decided to treat as a motion.”

“It’s the title of the whole last part, Professor,” Lena says. “And Waugh didn’t make it up. He took it from Chesterton. Father Brown says it, at the end of one of the stories — he caught the thief with an unseen hook and an invisible line, long enough to let him wander to the ends of the world, and still bring him back with a twitch upon the thread. Lady Marchmain reads it to the family after dinner, and nobody’s listening, and every one of them gets that twitch before the book’s over. Lord Marchmain gets it on his deathbed, with his hand. Sebastian gets it in Tunis — he ends up at the gate of a monastery carrying the monks’ bags, drunk half the time, and as near to God as anybody in the novel. Julia gets it at the same bedside. Charles gets it last. That isn’t a cage, Professor. A cage doesn’t let you go anywhere. That line lets you go everywhere. It’s just long.”

Hale relays it, and this time he doesn’t trim it: the hook, the line, the ends of the world, Tunis. He finishes on *It’s just long* in her cadence and not his, and then he sits back, and lets go of it. “The bishop in New York said very much the same,” he observes, “at three times the length, into a microphone that kept failing, God bless the bugger. I took it as a sign. I am told that is the correct response to a sign.”

It’s a good argument. It’s Thomas with the Chesterton showing — nature bent toward its end, and grace doing the bending — and he has heard her make it about Flannery O’Connor, and about the Saints, and once about a cat. He knows which joint the knife goes in. What he hears is an argument, and he has an answer for it.

choices.text: “A hook is still a hook. Tell her that.”
response: “And the fish doesn’t get a vote,” Jack says, to Hale. “Waugh calls it grace because Waugh’s the one holding the rod.”
Hale relays it with relish. “Mr. Costigan is on the side of the fish.”
“Tell him —” Lena says to Hale, and stops. She lays her pencil down across the book.
“Miss Broussard reserves her reply,” says Hale, and for a moment he sounds almost respectful.

choices.text: “Tell Miss Broussard that Father Brown caught a thief with that line. Waugh borrowed the tackle.”
response: “Plagiarism,” Hale says, purring. “Lovely. The chair adores a crime.” He gets up and writes PLAGIARISM on the whiteboard under the question, with a small, happy flourish, and sits down again.
“Tell Mr. Costigan the thief gave back the silver and went off a penitent,” Lena says, to Hale. “It’s the same story, Professor. That’s what the tackle is *for*.”

choices.text: “Tell her the thread’s the best thing in the book. It’s how Sebastian ends up at that gate.”
response: Hale relays it, and then, for the first time since he came in, says nothing clever after it.
“Yes,” Lena says, to Hale, quieter than she has been all afternoon.
“Good,” Hale says, after a while, to no one in particular, and looks displeased with himself for having said it.

choices.text: “Tell Miss Broussard that renunciation’s easy when it’s somebody else’s love you’re giving up.”
choices.key: In Hale’s seminar, through the chair, you told Lena renunciation’s easy when it’s somebody else’s love you’re giving up. Hale relayed it.
response: The table goes quiet as it went quiet at Hale’s, and Caleb’s stillness stops being a joke.

Hale could stop it. At Hale’s he stood up and did. Today he folds his hands on the roster and turns his head the long way round and sends it down the varnish word for word, beautifully, in the voice he keeps for Housman, so that it arrives at the window end with nothing knocked off it.
Lena sets her pencil down beside the book, parallel to it. “Professor,” she says, very pleasantly, “please tell Mr. Costigan I’ll take that under advisement.”
choices.cue: Lena heard every word of that.

s14b.slug: THURSDAY · 1:50 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE LAMP
body: At ten to two the sun gets all the way through for the first time today and lies down the table from the window as far as the middle, where Hale is sitting, and he shuts his eyes in it like a cat on a sill.
“The chair,” he says, without opening them, “would like to hear about the end. The chair has always been partial to endings. They are the only part of a book a man can’t revise by talking.”

“The Epilogue, Professor,” Lena says. “It’s the war. Charles is a captain, nobody’s painter anymore, and the army has moved his company into Brideshead without telling him where they were going. The soldiers have done to the house what soldiers do. And the chapel’s been opened up again, for the troops, and in front of the altar there’s a little red lamp — an ugly one, Waugh makes very sure we know it’s ugly — and it’s burning again. Somebody lit it. Charles goes in and kneels, and says a prayer, an old one, that he’s only just learned.” Her hand is on the cover. “And Julia isn’t in it, Professor. Have y’all noticed that? The book doesn’t even follow her. She did her part at her father’s bedside and the book let her go too. He kneels because Julia let him go. If she’d married him he’d be on a terrace in the south of France with a sketchbook and a grievance. Her no is what put him on his knees.”
Hale opens his eyes and relays it, all of it, down to *a grievance*. “Miss Broussard,” he adds, “offers the chair a terrace in the south of France, and declines it on Mr. Ryder’s behalf.”

The table holds still for it. The library copy has stopped crackling. Yusuf’s coffee is at his mouth and not going anywhere. In the sun the varnish shows every ring and scratch that thirty years of seminars have left in it, and at the window end the light has reached Lena’s book and the backs of her hands and stopped there, as if the sun had been told about the chair too.

It’s her best one. From the door end he can see the shape of it entire — the no as the hinge the book swings on, grace coming in by the wound — and he can see the place where it’s too neat, because it’s always too neat when she’s winning, and that’s where he goes in.
Jack has his answer in his mouth before Hale is through, and he waits for Hale to be through, because those are the rules, and they are the best rules anybody has made for him in a week.

choices.text: “He kneels because he’s grieving. Grief isn’t grace. Tell her.”
response: “Mr. Costigan says grief is not grace,” Hale tells the window, “and would like that minuted.”
“Tell him grief is the door grace uses, Professor,” Lena says. “It doesn’t knock at the front.”
Hale relays it and, for once, adds nothing.

choices.text: “Ask her who lit the lamp again. It wasn’t Julia. It wasn’t Charles.”
response: “An army chaplain,” Jack says, to Hale. “A builder. Some private from Liverpool with a box of matches. People who never read the book. The lamp doesn’t care whose bargain it was.”
Hale asks her. At the window end Lena takes a moment over it. “Tell him that’s the first true thing he’s said today,” she says.
“I’ll paraphrase,” says Hale.

choices.text: “Tell her the lamp is the ending. It’s hers.”
response: Hale relays it, and for once leaves his own adjective off the end.
At the window end Lena doesn’t answer. She nods, at the chair.

choices.text: “Tell Miss Broussard Charles is an army captain in a borrowed house. He kneels because it’s the only quiet room.”
response: Caleb laughs, and this time doesn’t try to stop.
Hale relays it with his face turned up to the window, the sun on it.
“Tell Mr. Costigan,” Lena says, to Hale, “that’s what everybody says the first time.”

s14c.slug: THURSDAY · 2:15 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE CARD

body.text: At a quarter past Hale closes his book on one finger. “Mr. Costigan has the text,” he says. “Miss Broussard has the book.”
At a quarter past Hale closes his book on one finger and is quiet for a while. “I have never once seen two people agree so thoroughly,” he says, “in order to avoid looking at each other.”
At a quarter past Hale closes his book on one finger. “Mr. Costigan has been very amusing. Miss Broussard has been right. The chair has enjoyed both. It’s a failing.”
At a quarter past Hale closes his book on one finger. “The chair is exhausted,” he says. “The chair would like a drink.” Nobody laughs; Caleb tries.

body: Then he stands and gets his coat off the back of the chair. “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace,” he tells the table, working an arm into a sleeve, apparently without hearing himself. “Miss Broussard will be absent for the next two weeks, attending to football and family.” He looks down the length of the table to the door end. “Mr. Costigan, you’ll have the table.”

The room gets up around him. Caleb unfreezes all at once. At the door he stops beside Jack’s chair, and in the twang he keeps for Scripture says, low, “And the chair spake unto them, saying, Go ye through me,” and waits to be thanked for it, and isn’t, and stays in the doorway doing up his backpack one strap at a time. The girl with the library copy is negotiating it back into her bag past the plastic. Yusuf puts his cup in the bin by the door and the pen in his shirt pocket, and stands there a moment with his hand on the pocket. “Half-duplex,” he says, mostly to himself. “One direction at a time, through a relay. It works. It’s just slow.” At the window end Lena is putting things away in an order: the Waugh, the pencil, the legal pad.

The sun has gone back in, and the eucalyptus has started up again outside the glass. Evan unclips the roster and says to the room, “Monday, then,” and to Jack, in the flattest Minnesota he has, “Table’s all yours, I guess,” and hears it as it comes out, and busies himself with the clip.
When Jack shifts on the chair he can feel the corner of the card through the paperback in his back pocket, a stiff place in Book Three.

choices.text: *Slide the card back down the table to her. Not a word.*
choices.key: Lena sent you a card asking you to New Orleans — you’d be welcome. After Hale’s, you slid it back down the table to her without a word.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes.
