Thursday there was a card in my box, cream, her mother’s, in her hand. Theo says I’m not coming. Her mother’s made up the twins’ room. American, Friday, 1:15. There’s a seat. I’d be welcome. At Hale’s we didn’t say a word to each other; everything went through the chair. After, I wrote *Take Julian.* under her name and left it in 217’s box.

response: He has a pen of his own in the Carhartt. He opens the card on his knee, under the lip of the table, and writes it below the L in his own hand, quick, and shuts it again before the ink can catch the light.
The lobby is empty except for Marcus and his crossword. 217’s box is at the far end of the wall, in the shade. He feeds the card through the slot in its brass door and hears it land.
It’s the same brass door as every other door on the wall, and it clicks the same. He notices that it does.

choices.text: *Keep it. Don’t answer at all.*
choices.key: Lena sent you a card asking you to New Orleans — you’d be welcome. You never answered it. It’s still in your *Brideshead*.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop. Thursday there was a card in my box, cream, her mother’s, in her hand. Theo says I’m not coming. Her mother’s made up the twins’ room. American, Friday, 1:15. There’s a seat. I’d be welcome. At Hale’s we didn’t say a word to each other; everything went through the chair. I didn’t answer it. It’s in my *Brideshead*.

response: He leaves the book where it is, with the card at Book Three, and stays in his chair under the clock while the room goes out past him. The paperback makes the shape in his pocket it always makes, a little thicker at the back than it was this morning.
She comes last. She goes by him at the door near enough that he hears her bag’s zipper run shut, and she doesn’t stop, and he doesn’t.
Evan waits at the switch with his clipboard under his arm until Jack notices that he’s the only one left in the room.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. When Lena and I went at each other across his table he stood up and stopped it, in a voice I’ve never heard out of him, and he wasn’t amused. Berkeley felt it through the floor. On the deck he said the table was his. He asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog. He may like to do it again. Gloria says he sat in the Anchor till two Sunday morning, reading her Housman. Thursday he made Lena and me speak only through him — all remarks to the chair. *Brideshead*: whether Julia’s right to send Charles away. He relayed every word. Lena’s gone two weeks, he says. I’ll have the table.

s14d.slug: THURSDAY · 2:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOADING DOCK

body.text: He comes back from Hollis by the lagoon path with the *Brideshead* in his back pocket and nothing in it now but his place, and goes around the side of Delgado to the dock.
He comes out of the lobby with the brass click still in his ear and goes around the side of the building, past the bike racks, to the dock.
He comes out of the lobby and goes around the side to the dock, with his own handwriting somewhere in the wall behind him, in the dark of a brass box.
He comes around the side of Delgado to the dock with the book in his back pocket and the card still in it, keeping his place.

body: The loading dock is where Delgado keeps the part of itself it doesn’t show: two dumpsters, a tower of blue milk crates, a pallet of paper towels shrink-wrapped against the weather, the grease barrel with its lid chained on. Somebody from the kitchen takes breaks out here: there’s a milk crate turned over by the steel door for a seat, and beside it a Folgers can of sand bristling with butts, and the smell of the habit has got into the cinderblock. A gull stands on the dumpster lid with its head on one side, auditing the grease barrel. A dining-hall truck is idling at the foot of the ramp with its back doors open. There’s weather coming in off the water; he can taste the salt even back here, and the truck’s exhaust lies along the concrete and won’t rise.

It starts in his mouth, as it always does — a dry place at the back of the tongue, a taste first, before his hands know anything about it — and then his hands know. The pack is in the left pocket of the Carhartt with the lighter tucked into the cellophane, and his fingers have found it before he’s decided they could. In the right pocket is the tin. He carried it to Ohio and back over Christmas, and it has ridden in this coat ever since, and he hasn’t opened it.

choices.text: *Light one.*
choices.key: After Hale’s you smoked one on the Delgado loading dock.
response: One Marlboro out of the soft pack, lit in the lee of the grease barrel on the second try. He smokes it standing at the edge of the dock with the truck’s exhaust coming up around his shoes, and it tastes like nothing for three drags and then like the garage on Glenwood in February. Six drags and it’s done.
He grinds it out on the dock’s steel edge and drops the butt in the dumpster, because somebody from the kitchen sweeps this dock, and it won’t be him.

choices.text: *Put it back.*
response: He puts the pack back in the Carhartt and zips the pocket over it, and stands there with both hands in his pockets until the driver comes out of the kitchen door with a hand truck of empty crates, loads them, slams the back doors, and takes the truck away down the ramp and the smell with it.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them.*
response: The tin comes out of the right-hand pocket warm from him. The hinge is stiff from not being asked to do anything. He opens it on the dock rail, out of the wind.

Eleven. He counts them a second time with one finger, the way Nonna counts change at the Giant Eagle, because the first count is never the one you sign for. Eleven. He closes it and puts it back where it rides.

s15.slug: THURSDAY · 3:40 PM · CAMPUS POINT LOT — THE SAAB, DANNY’S LETTER

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas he turned twenty-three. The unit let him call on a Tuesday, for his birthday, and he spent it on me. The block sang. I told him Theo asked me to New Orleans and I said no. He asked was it because of the TV one or the veil girl. I said neither. He said that’s two. Thursday his letter to Skye came in my box, in capitals, his number in the corner. She read it to me in the Saab. ‘My brother sings like a goat at a funeral.’ ‘He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.’

body: The wind has come around off the water since lunch, and it has teeth in it for the first time in weeks. The Campus Point lot is down to surfboards and Subarus and a girl changing under a beach towel with her elbows out. The Saab is nosed up to the rail at the far end with the top up for once and the radio off, and out past the point the islands have gone under a low gray lid.
His flannel from the Walk is on the back seat, folded on top of a Ralphs bag of things she forgot to pack Tuesday. She reaches back for it blind.

“This is coming with me,” she says. “It went to San Francisco. It can go to Santa Fe.” She puts it on over her T-shirt and buttons it to the throat, the sleeves down past her hands, and then goes into the Ralphs bag again and comes out with a gray sweatshirt and drops it in his lap. SWEETWATER ACADEMY CREW. “You get this. It’s the only honest thing I own.”
“For how long?”
“Sixteen days.” She points at it. “Washed.”
“By who?”
“By you. In the Delgado laundry room. I’ll know.”

He holds it up. The cuffs are chewed, both of them, and it smells like the Saab’s heater and whatever she puts in her hair. Her iPhone buzzes in the cup holder. She reads it off the screen in Corinne’s vowels — “*Thursday is a new day*” — and drops the phone in the Ralphs bag with the things she forgot, and folds the top of the bag over it.
He gives her the envelope. It’s been in the inside pocket of the Carhartt since the mailboxes this morning, Danny’s capitals marching across the front of it to her name.
“He said don’t read it,” Jack says. “I didn’t.”
“You held it up to a light.”
“Once.”
She opens it with a thumb under the flap, slowly, and takes out one sheet of lined paper written to the edges, and smooths it on the steering wheel, and reads it to him.

body.title: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
body.text:
MISS SKYE,
Thank you for writing me. Nobody writes me but Ma and the Professor and Gina, and Gina writes in colors.
You wrote my number bigger than the State of Ohio does. The CO read it out at mail call like a ballgame. I am famous on the range now. Reggie wants to know are you the girl on the yacht. I told him a lady don’t answer that.
Gina says you’re on TV Thursdays. We got one TV in the dayroom and it’s whatever the loudest guy wants, and the loudest guy wants wrestling. I’m working on him.
My brother sings like a goat at a funeral. If he ever sings to you, I’m sorry. I’m sorry ahead of time.
He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.
Write me back if you want. You don’t got to.
Push-ups 170.
DANNY
A555218

body: At Reggie she stops. “Who’s Reggie?”
“Portsmouth. He was Balthazar at Epiphany. The myrrh was a honey bun.”

“I love Reggie,” she says, and goes on. She gets as far as the goat and no farther. She puts her forehead down on the steering wheel, against the horn ring, and the horn doesn’t go off, and that sets her off again, and she has to sit up and wipe her eyes on the cuff of his flannel before she can find her place.
“Postmarked last week,” she says, turning the envelope over to check.
“He’s been in a car with me.”

She reads the rest. *He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him* she reads exactly as it’s written, no faster and no slower, and looks over at him across the gearshift before she goes on. There’s a sentence like that in every letter Danny sends. Jack watches the gray water out past the rail until she’s by it.
“*Push-ups one-seventy*,” she finishes.
It was a hundred and forty at Columbus Day.
She folds the letter along its old fold and holds it in her lap in both hands. “I’m writing him from New Mexico,” she says. “What can you send? To there.”
“Letters. Books — softcover, no staples. Theo called and asked. Photographs, regular ones. No Polaroids.”
“Why no Polaroids?”
“You can hide things in them. Between the layers.”
“Like what?”
“Ask Danny.”

She takes Dell’s pages off the dash and the Sharpie out of the cup holder and writes a list down the margin of the back page in capitals, as if capitals are the house style now: LETTERS. BOOKS — SOFT — NO STAPLES. PHOTOS (NOT POLAROID). Under it, after a minute, she adds WRESTLING?? and taps it twice.
“Would he want a picture?”
“Of you?”
“Of the horse. Dell’s horse. I’m going to make friends with it on my own time, so she doesn’t have to.” She writes HORSE under WRESTLING. “Would he put it up?”
“Where Reggie can see it,” Jack says. “Every day. Till Reggie’s sick of it.”
“Good,” she says.

response: “I was *there*, Youngstown. He’s being generous.”

And she does the goat. She does it at a funeral, with grief, with dignity, with the high part, her head back against the seat and one hand over her heart, and it’s him, it’s exactly him at Carrillo, and a surfer coming up from the beach stairs with his board under his arm stops beside the Saab to look in.
She starts the car doing it. Jack, who has given up, sits there with the sweatshirt in his lap, grinning at her like an idiot, while she does a second verse for the surfer.
“Is she okay?” the surfer asks Jack.
“She’s at a funeral,” Jack says, and Skye puts the Saab in reverse without breaking character, mourning, out of the space.

choices.text: “Write him back. He’ll read it forty times.”

“He reads mine out to Reggie. Reggie’s got a theory about the Pacific now. Money and fish.”
She writes DANNY — FROM NEW MEXICO at the top of the list, over the books. She slides his letter in between Dell’s pages at the very front, where the first day goes, and closes the pages on it.

She looks down at the capitals in her lap. “Your brother writes like he’s standing in front of me with his hands in his pockets.”
She starts the Saab and lets it idle at the rail, the heater coming up and the wind rocking the canvas top.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Tuesday at the Anchor he pitched me New Orleans on the placemats — the game at the Broussards’, a week, Bacchus — with six tickets printed and paid for, one with my name on it. Then he said he’s never asked me for anything, and he was asking. I said no. He folded the placemat in thirds and said it’s refundable. Thursday night he packed eleven coats for a warm city and left me a DVD for every night he’s gone. In the dark he asked, answer to what. I told him Nonna’s question, in her words.

body: Eleven coats lie across Theo’s bed with their sleeves arranged, shoulder to shoulder, like a lineup. Jack counts them from the doorway with the toothbrush still in his mouth. It comes out eleven.

On the windowsill the speaker is playing strings, something French and sad and expensive. The casement is open an inch on the dark and the eucalyptus, and Theo, in his shirtsleeves, is going down the row with a lint roller, a coat at a time, and doing the camel last, as if it might hear.

“Sixty-two degrees in New Orleans,” he says, “and every drop of humidity God ever made. Cashmere is out. Tweed would be a statement, and the statement would be *sweat*. I’m bringing the linen and the regret.”

body.text: Folding the linen, not looking up: “Laney says you slid it the length of Hale’s table. You could have just said no.”
Folding the linen, not looking up: “She showed Laney your penmanship.”
Folding the linen, not looking up: “Laney read it. That one was beneath you, Costigan.”
Folding the linen, not looking up: “Laney says she’s waiting for an answer.” “I know.”

body: Jack sits on the edge of his own bed. His half of 412 is a footlocker, a crucifix and a hook with a Carhartt on it, and he has nothing whatever to pack. On the closet door, across the room, a black Saints jersey hangs on a hanger, number 9, with the tags still on and a pocket square folded into the collar. “For the city,” Theo says, catching him looking. “A guest brings something.”
On the desk stands a stack of DVD cases, and every case has a yellow Post-it on its spine, in fountain pen. FRI. SAT. SUN — AFTER THE GAME. MON. The days go on down the pile to SUN 14.
“One for every night I’m gone,” Theo says, without turning around. “For a man who’s staying.”

Jack takes the top one. *The Third Man.* “A zither,” Theo says. “You’ll hate it by the end of the first reel and miss it by Monday. Wait for the last shot. A cemetery road, some trees, a woman. No one says a word. It’s the best thing anyone ever did with a road.” Under it, *Rififi*: “Half an hour of four men robbing a jeweler without a word of dialogue. You’ll find it restful.” Under that, SUN — AFTER THE GAME, *It’s a Wonderful Life*, and Jack looks up.
“For the loser,” Theo says. “Whoever it is. It works on both.”

Monday is *Paths of Glory*, and Jack says Monday looks grim. “Monday is Monday. I’m not a monster, Costigan. Go to the bottom.” The bottom is the fourteenth, *The Apartment*. “A man strains spaghetti through a tennis racket and a woman plays gin. You’ll be fine.”
“Skye leaves Saturday at six,” Jack says.

“Then you’re a man alone in a dormitory with a laptop and a stack of films,” Theo says. “I’m told that’s how monasteries get started.” He holds a coat up to the light, finds nothing wrong with it, and hangs it. “Pruitt will find you by Sunday. He has the instincts of a dowser.”
“Theo,” Jack says. “About Tuesday.”
“Tuesday was a pitch. Pitches die. It’s what they’re for.” Theo rolls the camel’s lapel and smooths it flat. “I’d apologize, but I already owe you a kidney, and I won’t be put into arrears.”
“You don’t owe me a kidney.”

“I owe everyone a kidney, Costigan. It’s how I stay solvent.” He tips his head at the desk. “The MacBook stays. It has the drive. You may use it. You may even ask. The password is *hollis*, lowercase, and if Priya ever learns it I will know where she got it.”
“I’ll ask.”

“I’ll know if you don’t.” He crosses to the mirror, where Nonna’s twenty is back in the frame, home from LA, and takes it out, and turns it over to the back, and tucks it in again. The iPhone is propped against a sleeve on the bedspread, and he reads the weather off it to the room. “Sixty-two, clear through Sunday. The Saints are getting the sun.” The little screen slides sideways under his finger to the next city. “My mother’s under the burn. They’re saying rain Friday.”
“Tell her hello.”
“She’ll ask if you’re eating,” Theo says. “They always ask.”

He zips ten of the coats into the long bag and leaves the camel over the desk chair for the morning, and moves Hollis from the nightstand to the sill beside the speaker. Jack hits the overhead on his way to bed. The streetlight lays the blind across the ceiling in stripes, and the strings come round to their theme again.
“There’s still a seat,” Theo says, from the dark.
“Goodnight, Theo.”
“Goodnight, Father Jack.”

body.text: “Last week I said it was love and you said *Yeah. It is.* The week before, she was *the answer*.” A pause from the other bed. “Answer to what, Costigan?”
“You’ve told me twice she’s the answer.” A pause from the other bed. “Answer to what, Costigan?”
“You keep saying *the answer* like it’s on a plaque.” A pause from the other bed. “Answer to what, Costigan?”

choices.text: Tell him the question. All of it.
choices.key: In the dark Theo asked, answer to what. You told him Nonna’s real question, all of it, in her words. When he asked which one, you didn’t answer.
response: Jack says it to the ceiling. It comes out in his grandmother’s accent, the only one he has for it, and he had not known it would come at all: Christmas night, the phone lit in his hand, her beads going. “*Due ragazze.* Two girls. *Quale ti fa pregare.* Which one makes you pray.”
The blind stripes lie on the ceiling and do nothing. When Theo speaks it is very low. “*Which* one.”
Jack doesn’t answer. Theo waits a long time in the dark, and then he turns over to face the wall.

choices.text: Tell him, and then tell him the answer.
choices.key: In the dark Theo asked, answer to what. You told him Nonna’s real question, and then the answer: she does.
response: “*Quale ti fa pregare.*” It is the first time he has said it in her words, and it comes out in Nonna’s accent, as she said it on Christmas night over her beads. “Which one makes you pray. It’s what she asked me. And she does.”
“*Which* one,” Theo says.
“I just told you.”
“You did.” The speaker, still on, clicks off at the end of the record.

choices.text: “Pasta, Theo. She asked about pasta.” Then the real one.
choices.key: In the dark Theo asked, answer to what. You told him Nonna asked about pasta. Then you gave him the real question, and when he asked which one, you told him to ask you in the morning.
response: “Liar,” says Theo.
So Jack gives him the real one, in Italian and then in English, all of it, the first time he has said all of it aloud: *Due ragazze. Quale ti fa pregare.* Two girls. Which one makes you pray.
“*Which* one.”
“Ask me in the morning.”

“In the morning I’ll be a man with a garment bag.” A long breath from the other bed. “Noted,” Theo says, kindly, and lets him have it. Outside the window the eucalyptus goes in a south wind that has brought nothing yet.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Tuesday at the Fishbowl she passed me the popcorn and then remembered not to. Wednesday they were all in 412 when I came back for my jacket: her birthday, she said; Kevin said the fourteenth, Valentine’s. A party for her on Bacchus Sunday, at the Broussards’. Friday at the curb: “Have a nice weekend, fireman.”

journal.title: New Orleans
journal.text: The Saints are in the Super Bowl. Friday morning Theo, Lena, Laney, Kevin and Margot left for New Orleans in a black car with the driver who took Theo to his First Communion: the game at the Broussards’, then a week, then Bacchus. Home the fifteenth. Six tickets; one had my name on it. Theo says he’ll hold my seat. I told him don’t. Sunday I’m on Doug’s futon with Yusuf.

body: The wind has gone around to the south, warm, with dust in it, under a high white sky. Every palm on the Delgado lawn leans toward the 101. At the curb a black Lincoln Navigator has taken the whole red zone with its hazards going, and beside its open tailgate stands a man in a gray overcoat who has plainly been waiting for Theo Vance most of his life.

On the top step Priya Raman has appeared in her RA lanyard with a stopwatch and a laminated card. “Per the Residential Life Handbook,” she tells the driver, “a vehicle in the red zone has five minutes.”
“Miss,” says the man in the overcoat, “I am a professional.”
“So is the handbook.” She starts the watch.

“Arturo,” Theo announces, coming down the steps with the camel coat over his arm, and says it to Jack as though introducing a cathedral. “Arturo drove me to my First Communion and my first arrest, Costigan. Both were misunderstandings.”
“Mr. Costigan,” Arturo says, and takes the garment bag out of Theo’s other hand before it can be explained.

Jack stops on the third step down from the doors and goes no farther. He has come down because staying upstairs would have been its own kind of message, and he has no message. The loading is a negotiation. Laney’s four bags go in largest first under Arturo’s direction (“Arturo, darlin’, that one rides with me. It has my *face* in it”), and her garment bag is carried down by Laney herself and laid on top like a patient. Margot’s one black duffel goes in last and takes up less room than Laney’s hat. Kevin’s roller bag has a tag on the handle in his mother’s marker: KEVIN TRAN — CALL MA WHEN YOU LAND. Theo casts the seats like a picture: Margot behind the driver, Laney in the middle where the light is best, Kevin on the curb side so he can get out first and check everything.
Margot shakes Jack’s hand once, like a colleague’s. “I’m told it’s a matriarchy disguised as a parade,” she says. “I’ll be taking notes.”

Kevin goes in for the handshake and gives it up halfway, and it becomes a hug with the handshake still caught in the middle. “Disclosure,” he says, into the shoulder of the Carhartt. “This is a hug. I’m not charting it.”

Laney comes down the steps in a gold scarf she has bought for the cameras and walks straight up to Jack, and her hands go to the collar of the Carhartt where it’s folding under and flatten it. “Have a nice weekend, fireman,” she says, sunglasses pushed up into her hair, smiling with every tooth. She looks at her own hands. The sunglasses come down, and she goes to the car, and in the second row of the Navigator she is a pair of black lenses behind tinted glass, pointed at the steps. Jack stands with the collar flat where she left it.

Lena comes down the steps last, with her duffel over her shoulder and the pie box in both hands. She passes him on the step close enough that the corner of the box nearly brushes his sleeve. She doesn’t say anything, and he doesn’t. Arturo takes the duffel, and the box, and she climbs into the third row.
On the bench by the bike rack Yusuf Noorzai has been reading *Nine Stories* since before the Lincoln came, and has not turned a page. He turns one now.
At the car door Kevin counts off the party on one finger, as he counts everything. “Five,” he says. “That’s correct.” The smile comes up a little late.

Theo is the only one still talking. “Pecan,” he says. “I told Gloria on Tuesday. She boxed one for the grandmother. Gloria has views on matriarchs.” He stands at the open door with the camel coat, and then he stops talking. “I’ll hold your seat.”
“Don’t.”
“I’ll hold it anyway.”

In the third row the seat beside Lena is empty. Theo leans in and lays the camel coat across it, collar up, and brings the belt over the coat and clicks it home. Then he gets in up front beside Arturo, and Arturo shuts the doors one at a time, and the Navigator goes down the drive.
At the stop sign at the end of the drive the Lincoln’s brake lights come on and stay on a little longer than the sign needs, and then it turns toward the 101.
Priya clicks the stopwatch. “Four-forty,” she announces, and writes it on the card, and goes in.
The RAZR goes off in the pocket of the Carhartt, three times in a minute, and Jack reads them standing on the step in the wind from the south.
